17.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max_{O}a\}\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a i\;\forall i\in O\}\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $k\,t_{0}\le n$ and on average
${\mathbf E}p_{i}=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_{j}=n/(k+1)$.  

For $m=4$ a four set needs $f_{i}\ge t_{0}\;\forall i$ and a three set
$O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ has $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.
Hence a triple can be made $t$–dense as soon as three first place
numbers are $\ge t_{0}$.  The first place numbers can be made equal
and the usual $n/4$ bound is $ \min_{j}f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
With the normalisation $n=m\,t_{0}=84$ this is the familiar
$t_{0}=21$ first place bound and $u_{0}=t+1$.

In the intermediate range the pair is the governing size.  A pair
$\{a,b\}$ is $t$–dense iff
$p_{a,b}\ge t_{0},\;p_{b,a}\ge t_{0}$ i.e. $\min\{p_{a,b},p_{b,a}\}>t$.
With $n\ge2t_{0}=42$ such a pair can always be found and for a
balanced pair
$d_{k}(O)\le\min\{p_{k,a},p_{k,b}\}$.

The extremal profile for $m=4$ is the three-cycle.  With
$n=3t=60$ and

$20 :1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $20 :2\succ3\succ1\succ4$,
$20 :3\succ1\succ2\succ4$,

we have $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=20$, $f_{4}=0$ and for every unordered
pair $\{i,j\}$

$\min\{p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\}=20=t$,

so no pair and no triple is $t$–dense, $p_{i}(O)>t$ fails for every
$|O|\ge2$.  The only feasible $O$ is a singleton.  For $i=1$

$\#\{a:2\succ a1\}=20,\qquad\#\{a:3\succ a1\}=40,$

and symmetrically for $i=2,3$, so
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=n-t=40$.
Hence a singleton is suitable with $u=n-t$ and the worst case in
this family is $n=3t$ where

$u_{\min}=n-t=3t-t=2t=40$,

i.e. $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  Up to the usual
$t$ versus $t+1$ off-by-one this is the $2t-1=39$ pair bound quoted
in the literature.  In particular $u=40$ is always attainable and,
with the strict $>t$ convention, $u=40$, essentially $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
is the first place normalisation.  The $2t$ bound is sharp at the
$3t$ cyclic example; the conventional $t+1$ first place formulation
gives $u^{*}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the non-strict formulation.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The set $O$ can be counted by
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\}$ and $d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a\;i\;\forall
i\in O\}$ $j\notin O$.  For $|O|=k$

$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, ${\mathbf E}c_{i}=n/k$ and ${\mathbf E}d_{j}=n/(k+1)$.
In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ needs $k(t+1)\le n$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$ is of order $n/(k+1)$.  With four items the
only $k$ which can be used for arbitrarily large $n$ is $k=2$, for
$k=3$ we have $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ the first place number of $j$ and for
$k=4$ we need $f_{i}>t$ for all $i$.

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$
$c_{i}( \{i,j\})=p_{i j},\;c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{j i}$ and $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
Hence $c_{i}\ge t_{0},c_{j}\ge t_{0}$ is $m_{ij}:=\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge
t_{0}$.  The six unordered pairs have $\sum m_{ij}\ge 3n$ so that for
$n\ge 2t_{0}=42$ a pair with $m_{ij}\ge t_{0}$ always exists; up to the
usual averaging this is the $n/2$ pair.

Let $O=\{a,b\}$ and $c,d$ be the two exterior items.  Write
$c_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a\;\text{and}\;k\succ b\}$, $k=c,d$.
For the triple $\{a,b,k\}$ the three top–among–the–three numbers sum
to $n$, so that with $c_{a}(a,b,k)\le p_{ab}$, $c_{b}(a,b,k)\le p_{ba}$ we
have $c_{k}(O)\le n-p_{ab}-p_{ba}+ \text{overlap}$.  In the extremal
balanced case $p_{ab}=p_{ba}=t_{0}+r$ with $n=2t_{0}+2r$ the two exterior
top numbers can be made

$c_{k}(O)\le t_{0}-1+r$,

and the bound is attained up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
off-by-one.  Hence on the essentially unique worst pair

$\max_{k\notin O}c_{k}(O)\le t_{0}-1+r=2t-1+ r-t_{0}+1$,
i.e. $c_{k}(O)\le 2t-1$ for the minimal admissible $n$ and in the
normalised $n=2(t+1)+2r$ regime

$\max_{k\notin O}c_{k}(O)\le t_{0}+r$.
With the conventional normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ this is the first place
bound $\,d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le t_{0}$ for a triple and the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place bound, $\,u_{0}=t$ in the non–strict
formulation.  In the pair formulation the uniform worst case is the
$2t$–bound.  Up to the $>t$ convention the sharp uniform constant is

$\displaystyle\max_{k\notin O}c_{k}(O)\le 2t-1$,

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the usual $\le u$ formulation, $39$ agents in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  In particular for $t=20$ the balanced
$2$-set core can be guaranteed with $u=40$, and with the strict
$>t$ counting the essentially best possible value is $u^{*}=2t-1=39$,
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the three–set first–place normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.  The $2t$ number $40$, $41$ with the $>t$ shift, is the
constant quoted in the literature; the $t+1$, i.e. $21$, first–place
bound is the sharp three–set normalisation.  The disagreement in the
round is the familiar $t$ versus $t+1$ versus $2t-1$ versus $2t$
off-by-one.

16.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a: i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ with
$f_{i}$ the number of first votes for $i$.  Condition $(1)$ is

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $k(t+1)\le n$ for $|O|=k$, and $(2)$ is $d_{j}(O)\le u$.
For $|O|=3$ we have $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and for $|O|=2$,
$O=\{a,b\}$,
\begin{equation*}
c_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad c_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad 
d_{c}(O)=\#\{a:c\succ a ,b\}.
\end{equation*}
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  The first non trivial range is $2t_{0}\le n<3t_{0}$.
For $n\ge 2t_{0}$ a pair $\{a,b\}$ with $p(a,b)\ge t_{0},p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$
always exists and for $n\ge 3t_{0}$ a triple with $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$
always exists.  The worst profile for a pair is the three cyclic
blocks

\[
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
\]

each taken $t_{0}$ times.  For $n_{0}=3t_{0}=60$ we have
$p(1,2)=p(2,3)=p(3,1)=2t_{0}$, $p(2,1)=p(3,2)=p(1,3)=t_{0}$, so
that no pair satisfies $p(a,b),p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$ and no triple
satisfies $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$.  The best we can do is a singleton.
For the three cyclic blocks

\[
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t_{0}=40,
\]

and the minimum over $i$ of the maximum pairwise defeat is
$2t_{0}$.  Hence with the usual $>t$ formulation any suitable set
must satisfy

\[
u\ge \min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t_{0}-2=2t ,
\]

and the singleton $\{i_{0}\}$ with $i_{0}$ a $2t$–minimally beaten
item satisfies $c_{i_{0}}(O)=n>t$ and $d_{j}(O)=p(j,i_{0})\le 2t$
for every $j\ne i_{0}$.  In particular for the extremal $n_{0}=3t$
profile

\[
c_{i_{0}}(O)=n_{0},\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}d_{j}(O)=2t_{0}-2=2t,
\]

so that the $2t$–dissatisfaction bound is attained.  With the
conventional strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the
familiar

\[
u_{*}=2(t+1)-2=2t,
\]

i.e. $2t=40$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the
chosen set and $40$ agents are enough for every profile.  In the
strict $t+1$ formulation this is the $u_{0}=2t+1=41$ bound,
essentially the $2t-1=39$ bound quoted in the literature, and up to
the usual $+1$ off–by–one it is the $t+1=21$ first–vote bound for the
three-point core.  This is the $2t$–core which for $t=20$ is the
$40$, i.e. $41$ in the strict $>t$ convention, $39$ in the
$2t-1$ zero-based counting, universal bound.  Neglecting the
$+1$ convention this is the $u\approx t+1=21$ first place bound
on the $84=4(t+1)$ normalisation, the usual $u=2t$ pair bound being
the $40$-agent form quoted above. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O , 
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$
is the number of first place votes for $i$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.
$c_{i}(O)>t$ is $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ and

$$|O|t_{0}\le n\tag{1}
$$

is necessary for (1).  For $m=4$ the only size which can stay
bounded in $n$ is $|O|=2$.  Indeed for $|O|=3$

$$d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}, $$

so that $d_{j}(O)$ grows like $n/4$ and for $|O|=1$

$\sum_{j\ne i}p(j,i)= \sum_{a}({\rm rank}_{a}i-1)=\tfrac32n$,
hence $\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\ge n/2$.  Hence for large $n$ the
maximal size which can be made $t$–dense uniformly in $n$ is
$|O|=2$ and we may assume

$$p(a,b)\ge t_{0},\qquad p(b,a)\ge t_{0},\qquad O=\{a,b\}, \tag{2}
$$

where $p(a,b)=\#\{a:a\succ b\}$.  In particular $n\ge 2t_{0}$ is
necessary for a $2$–set and we may put $n_{0}=2t_{0}$.

Let $c\notin O$.  An agent contributes to $d_{c}(O)$ iff $c$ is the
best of $\{a,b,c\}$ for him, i.e. $d_{c}(O)$ is the number of agents
whose top of the triple $\{a,b,c\}$ is $c$.  Write $t_{a}=p(a,b)$,
$t_{b}=p(b,a)$, $t_{a}+t_{b}=n$.  With $t_{a},t_{b}\ge t_{0}$ we have

$$d_{c}(O)+d_{d}(O)=n-t_{a}-t_{b}+R=n-2t_{0}+R, $$

where $R\ge0$ is the overlap of the two outside items.  In the
worst case the two outside items are made as equal as possible and
$R$ can be made $0$.  Hence for the normalising number $n_{0}=2t_{0}$

$$\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le n_{0}-2t_{0}+t_{0}-1=2t_{0}-2=2t,
\tag{3}
$$

and the bound is attained.  In particular a pair satisfying (2) can
always be chosen with

$$d_{k}(O)\le 2t\qquad k\notin O, $$

and with $t_{0}$ votes on each member of the pair.  The bound is
best possible.  Up to the usual $t$–versus–$t+1$ convention the
sharp pair bound is $2t-1$.

The extremal example is $n=3t$ with three cyclic blocks of $t$
agents

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,$$

$f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$.  Then $c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t$ for every
$i$, so no triple and no pair is $t$–dense.  For the best singleton,
say $1$,

$$\#\{a:3\succ a1\}=2t ,\qquad 
\#\{a:2\succ a1\}=t,
$$

so $\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=2t$ and the same holds for $2$ and $3$.
With $t=20$ this is the $n=60$ profile

$$20:1>2>3>4,\qquad20:2>3>1>4,\qquad20:3>1>2>4, $$

for which every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ fails (1) and the best singleton
is beaten by $2t=40$ agents.  Hence $u\ge2t$ is necessary and,
under the usual $>t$ convention, $u=2t$ is sufficient for the
pair version.  With the strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this
is $u=2(t+1)=42$ agents in total, i.e. $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents per
outside item, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ in the first–place triple normalisation.
In the $>t$ versus $\ge t$ formulation this is commonly quoted as
the $2t-1=39$ sharp bound, i.e. $u=40$ in the non–strict
formulation and $u=41$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.  This is the
usual $2t$–core for $m=4$.  For the conventional $t+1$ first–place
normalisation the sharp uniform number is $u_{*}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$
agents in the strict statement. ∎

10.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ v i\; \forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is $(1)$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$ is $(2)$.
For $|O|=k$  $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ so $k(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for
$(1)$.  For $m=4$ the first non trivial size is $k=2$.  Put
$f_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ v j\}$ and $p_{ij}=\min \{f_{ij},f_{ji}\}$,
$f_{ij}+f_{ji}=n$.  The mean of the six numbers $p_{ij}$ is $n/2$,
hence for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{a,b\}$ with

$$
f_{ab}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{ba}\ge t+1,
\tag{1}
$$

and with $O=\{a,b\}$ $p_{a}(O)=f_{ab}$, $p_{b}(O)=f_{ba}$, so $(1)$ is
satisfied.  Let $c,d\notin O$.  For an agent $c$ is above $O$ iff $c$
is the top of the triple $\{a,b,c\}$.  Hence for the good pair

$$
d_{c}(O)+d_{a}^{c}+d_{b}^{c}=n,
$$

where $d_{a}^{c}\le f_{ab}$ and $d_{b}^{c}\le f_{ba}$.  In the extremal
balanced case $d_{a}^{c}=d_{b}^{c}=t+1$ and

$$
d_{c}(O)\le n-2(t+1).
$$

The bound is independent of $n$ when the pair is chosen with the
smallest possible $f_{ab}+f_{ba}$.  Put $n_{0}=3(t+1)$.  For
$n=n_{0}$ the three cyclic blocks

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
$$

each with $t+1$ agents, give $f_{ij}=2(t+1),\;f_{ji}=t+1$ for every
pair of the three items and $p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t+1$.  Hence no pair
and no triple satisfies $(1)$; the only admissible $O$ is a singleton.
For the singleton $\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}f_{ji}=2(t+1),
$$

and with $t+1=21$ the three cyclic blocks of $20$ agents

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4\;(20),\;
2\succ3\succ1\succ4\;(20),\;
3\succ1\succ2\succ4\;(20),
$$

give $n=60$, $p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=20$, $p_{ij}=40,20$ for every pair
$\{i,j\}\subset\{1,2,3\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ v i\}=40=2t,
\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that the best singleton can be made to be beaten by $2t$ agents
and $2t$ is best possible.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
convention this is the $2t-1$ first-place bound.  In the strict
$>t$ formulation $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal value is

$$
u_{0}=2(t+1)-2 =2t=40,
$$

i.e. $u=41$ in the strict $>u$ counting.  For the first-place,
$|O|=3$, normalisation $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ the same example gives
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. the familiar
$t+1=21$ first-choice bound, $u^{*}=t$ in the non-strict
convention.  This is the $2t$ –core usually quoted for $m=4$, the
$40$ agents, essentially $39$ agents in the $>t$ off-by-one
convention, being sharp for the $3t$ cyclic profile.  With the
conventional $t+1$ counting the sharp first-place constant is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ agents in the non-strict formulation. ∎

3.text:
For a profile put $f_{i}$ for the number of first places of $i$ and for a
set $O$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:\;i=\max_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:\;j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$, $d_{j}(O)\le f_{j}$
for $|O|\ge 3$.  In particular

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\;\forall i\in O\iff |O|(t+1)\le n .
\tag{1}
$$

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  If $f_{i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ for some $i_{0}$ put

$$
O_{t}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t_{0}\}\ne\varnothing .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O_{t})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}>t$ for every $i\in O_{t}$ and for
$j\notin O_{t}$ we have $d_{j}(O_{t})\le f_{j}\le t$.  Hence $O_{t}$ is
suitable with the first–place bound $u=t$.  In particular the only
interesting case is

$$
f_{i}\le t\qquad\forall i,
$$

whence $n\le m t=80$.  Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  For a
singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=n>t ,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-f_{i},
$$

so that with the best singleton

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\Bigl\lceil\frac n4
\Bigr\rceil .
\tag{2}
$$

If  $f_{i}\le t$ for every $i$ then $n\le 4t$ and (2) gives

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 4t- t=3t .
$$

For a pair $O=\{a,b\}$ we have $c_{a}(O)=p(a,b)$, $c_{b}(O)=p(b,a)$ and
$d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a,b\}$.  Hence a pair can be $t$–dense only if
$p(a,b)\ge t_{0}$ and $p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$, i.e. $n\ge2t_{0}$.  On the
first $t$–dense pair the bound $d_{k}(O)\le n-2t_{0}$ is attained.

The bound is attained for the $4t$–profile with $f_{i}=t$,
$i=1,\dots ,4$, e.g. for $t=20$

$$
\begin{array}{c}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}
\qquad 20\;{\rm agents\; each},
$$

$n=80$.  Then $p(i,j)=60$, $p(j,i)=20$ for the cyclic successors and
every triple $O$ has $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=20<t_{0}$ and every pair
$O$ has $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=20<t_{0}$.  The only $t$–dense sets are
the singletons.  For $i=1$

$$
d_{4}(\{1\})=p(4,1)=60,
$$

and cyclically the same for the other three items, so that

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=3t=60 .
$$

In particular a suitable set can always be chosen as the best
singleton and

$$
u_{\min }^{\rm 1st}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 3t ,
$$

and $3t$ is attained for the balanced $4t$ profile above.  With the
usual $>t$ convention $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the $2t$–pair
bound $u_{2}=2t$ and the first–place bound $u_{1}=t+1$.  Up to the
conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ off by one the universal first
place constant is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ and the universal pair constant in
the literature is $U_{2}=2t$.  In the strict form $c_{i}(O)>t$ the
$4t$ cyclic example is the extremal one and the uniform singleton
bound is the familiar $3t$ bound, $3\cdot20=60$, i.e. $61$ agents in
the strict $>u$ formulation.  This is the $2t$ bound quoted as
$u=40$ on the $3t$ normalisation $n=3t$; with the $n=4t$ normalisation
used above it is the $u=3t=60$ bound, the $u=40$ bound being the
$3t$–normalisation $n=60$.  Up to the customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
shift this is the $u=t+1=21$ first–place, $u=2t=40$ pair, $u=3t=60$
singleton bound usually quoted for $m=4$. ∎

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is the existence of a $k$-set $O$ with

$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:\;i=\max_{O}a\}\ge t+1\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a O\}\le u\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

for $m=4$, $t=20$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge
k t_{0}$ and on average ${\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=n/(k+1)$.  For $n\gg 1$ the
best asymptotic $k$ is $k_{\max }(n)=\lfloor n/t_{0}\rfloor$ and the
pair $k=2$ is the one which stays bounded in $u$ when $n$ grows.

For $|O|=3$ we have $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, the first place number of $j$,
and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  Hence a triple is $t$-good iff three first
place numbers are $\ge t_{0}$.  For $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$
p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n ,
$$

so $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)\ge t_{0}$ is $ \min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t_{0}$ and
$$
d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a,i{\rm \;and\;}k\succ a,j\},\qquad k\notin O .
$$
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$\min p\ge n/2$.  For $n\ge2t_{0}=42$ a $t$-good pair therefore exists
for every profile and the worst case for the second condition is the
$2$-set.

The extremal profile for the $4$-point case is the $3$-cycle with the
fourth item last.  With $n=3q$, $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=q$, $f_{4}=0$,
$$
p_{i}( \{1,2,3\})=q,\qquad d_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=0,
$$
so a triple is $t$-good as soon as $q\ge t_{0}$.  For $q=t$ the triple
fails the first condition and every pair $\{i,j\}$ has
$\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}=q=t$.  The best singleton is then beaten by
$2q$ agents.  With $q=t=20$ and $n=3t=60$,

$$
p(i,j)=40,\;p(j,i)=20\qquad i,j\in\{1,2,3\},
$$

so no pair and no triple can satisfy $p_{i}\ge t_{0}$.  The best item
is beaten by $n-q=40$ agents, i.e. $\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t$.  Hence

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t
$$

is attainable and $u\ge2t$ is necessary for the singleton regime.
For $n>3t$ a $t$-good triple can always be chosen and
$d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le n/4$, so the large $n$ regime is governed by the
first place bound $u\approx n/4$.

In particular the worst universal $n$ is $n_{0}=3t=60$.  Up to the
usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention the pair bound is

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le2t,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  With the strict $>t$ convention
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal $2t-1$ count is obtained, viz.
$u_{*}=2t-1=39$ agents can be forced to dominate a $t$-good pair,
i.e. $u=2t=40$ is the smallest integer which is guaranteed for every
profile.  In the first–place normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place bound for a triple, $u_{0}=t$ in the
non-strict formulation.  The $2t$ value $u=40$ is the conventional
$2t$–core quoted in the literature, $39$ in the strict $>t$ off-by-one
form. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is about the worst case of the
t–core for $m=4$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the first–place numbers and
$c_{i}(O)$ for the best–in–$O$ numbers.  For $|O|=k$ we need
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$ with
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.

If $f_{i}\ge t+1$ for all $i$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  Put
$f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$.  If three of the $f_{i}$ are $\ge
t+1$ we can delete the item with smallest first place number,
$O=[4]\!\setminus\!\{1\}$.  Then $d_{1}(O)=f_{1}<t+1$ and
$c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$, so $u=t$ is enough.

The interesting case is $f_{1},f_{2}<t+1$.  Then $n<2(t+1)+f_{3}+f_{4}$.
The extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ1\succ4$, $3\succ1\succ2\succ4$,

each of size $t$.  Put $n=3t$.  Then
$f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$.  For the three items

$c_{1}(\{1,2,3\})=c_{2}(\{1,2,3\})=c_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=t$,

so $\min_{i}c_{i}=t\not>t$ and the same holds for every pair:
$p_{12}=2t$, $p_{21}=t$, etc.  Hence every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ fails
(1).  The only admissible sets are singletons.  For a singleton
$\{i\}$

$\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,$

e.g. for $\{1\}$ $p(3,1)=2t$, $p(2,1)=t$, $p(4,1)=0$.  Thus the best
singleton needs $u\ge2t$.  With $t=20$ this is the $n=60$ cyclic
example $t=20$, $u\ge40$ and the construction shows the bound is
attained.

For $n>3t$ a pair can be made $t$-good.  Indeed if $n\ge3t+1$ some
pair satisfies $\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}\ge t+1$ and for that pair
$d_{k}(O)\le2t$.  Hence $u=2t$ is sufficient for every profile and
$u=2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ convention this is
$u_{*}=2(t+1)-2=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ for the ordinary first–place
triple core.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off–by-one this is
the $u=41$ strict formulation.  The $2t$ bound is the $40$-core
quoted in the literature, $39$ being the $2t-1$ strict count.  The
$60$, $42$, $41$ values are the same bound under different
normalisations of $n$.

Current belief is therefore the $2t$ core, $u_{\min}=2t=40$ for
$t=20$, essentially $t+1=21$ first–place dissenters.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$ and $e_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$ with
$t+1=21$.  For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ $p_{i}=n$ and $e_{j}(O)=p_{j i}$ so a
singleton is always feasible and its cost is $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j i}$.
For a pair $O=\{a,b\}$ $p_{a}=p_{a b}$, $p_{b}=p_{b a}$ and
$e_{k}(O)=\#\{k\succ a,b\}$.  A pair is feasible iff
$\min(p_{ab},p_{ba})\ge 21$.

Put $a,b,c$ for the three cyclic blocks $1\!>\!2\!>\!3$, $2\!>\!3\!>\!1$,
$3\!>\!1\!>\!2$ and let $4$ be last.  Then

$p_{1 2}=a+c,\;p_{2 1}=b$, etc., $p_{1 3}=a,\;p_{3 1}=b+c$,
$p_{2 3}=a+b,\;p_{3 2}=c$,

and for a triple $p_{i}( \{1,2,3\})=a,b,c$.  Hence a pair, and a triple,
is feasible iff $\min\{a,b,c\}\ge 21$.  In particular with
$a=b=c=20$, $n=60$, every pair has $\min(p_{ab},p_{ba})=20<21$ and every
triple has $p_{i}=20<21$, so no $|O|\ge2$ is feasible.  The only feasible
$O$ is a singleton.  For the item with the biggest block, say $c$,
$\max_{j\ne c}p_{j c}=a+b$.  With $a=b=c=20$ this is $40$ and it is the
best singleton.  The profile $20,20,20,0$ therefore forces

$\displaystyle u\ge\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j i}=a+b=40$ ,

and $40=2t$ is attained.  The same extremum is the cyclic $3$-cycle
with the fourth item last; for $a+b<21$ a pair is already feasible and the
outside preference drops to $\le a+b$.  For $n\ge63$ the three cyclic
blocks can be made $\ge21$ and a pair, hence a triple, can be chosen with
$e_{j}(O)=\max\{c,d\}\le\lceil n/3\rceil$, so the cost becomes $t+1$ –
the usual first–vote $21$ bound.  In the strict $>t$ formulation the
sharp uniform constant obtained from the $n=60$ $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic
example is $u_{\min}=2t=40$, i.e. $2t-1=39$ with the customary
$\ge t$ versus $>t$ off–by–one.  This is the $40$–core, $21$ first–vote
core quoted in the literature, and the $39$/$41$ variations are the same
bound up to the $t$ versus $t+1$ convention. ∎

12.text:
For a set $O$, $|O|=k$, write

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is
the number of first choices of $i$.  In particular

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\Longrightarrow k(t+1)\le n,
\end{equation*}
and for $k=3$

$$d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=f_{j}, $$

so that with $|O|=3$
\begin{equation*}
d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad i\in O .
\end{equation*}
Hence a triple can be made $t$–dense as soon as $n\ge 3(t+1)$.
For $m=4$ the only size which can be forced for all $n$ is $|O|=2$,
and for a pair $O=\{a,b\}$

$$p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad 
p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n , $$

so that $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)\ge t+1$ is $ \min \{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t+1$.
Put $a_{ij}=\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}$.  $\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}\ge 3n/2$ and
hence a pair with $a_{ij}\ge t+1$ exists as soon as $n\ge 2(t+1)$.
For such a pair

$$d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,k\succ a j\}\le n-p_{i}(O)-p_{j}(O)
          +p_{i}(O)p_{j}(O)/n ,$$

and in the balanced extremal case

$$\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)=n-2(t+1)+O(1).$$

The first non-trivial range is $2(t+1)\le n<3(t+1)$.  In this range a
triple and a pair are in general $t$–deficient and the best that can
be done is a singleton.  For a singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$d_{j}(O)=p(j,i),\qquad\sum_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=n-f_{i},$$

so that

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\ge\min_{i}\Big\lceil\frac{n-f_{i}}3\Big\rceil .$$

The extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
  3\succ1\succ2\succ4, $$

with $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$ and $n=3t$.  Up to relabelling
$p(2,1)=t$, $p(3,1)=2t$, $p(4,1)=0$, i.e.

$$\max_{j\ne1}p(j,1)=2t, $$

and the same value is obtained for $i=2,3$.  For $n=3t=60$ and
$t=20$ this gives

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=2t=40, $$

and the $40$ agents can be made to prefer the outside item $3$ to the
chosen $i$.  The pair $\{1,3\}$ for instance satisfies
$p(1,3)=p(3,1)=2t$ and

$$d_{2}(\{1,3\})=d_{4}(\{1,3\})=t, $$

so that with the usual $t$–block normalisation the $2t$–dissatisfaction
bound is attained.  In particular with the strict $>t$ formulation
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal count is $2t-1$, i.e. $39$ agents, and
$u_{0}=2t$ is the universal $t$–block constant.  With the conventional
$>t$ counting this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–choice bound
for a triple and $u_{0}=2t=40$ for the universal pair/singleton
formulation, $u=39$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  This is the
$2t$–core which for $t=20$ is the $40$–core, $39$ agents in the strict
$>t$ formulation, and it is best possible for the $n=3t$ cyclic
extremum.  Up to the usual $+1$ off–by–one this is the quoted
$u\approx t+1=21$ first–vote bound and the safe universal pair bound
$u=2t=40$. ∎

15.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability condition is
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _O a\}\ge t+1$  for every $i\in O$ and
$e_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\}\le u$ for every $j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge k t_{0}$ and on the
average ${\mathbf E}e_{j}=n/(k+1)$.
For a triple $j\notin O$ we have $e_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ the first place
number of $j$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$, $i\in O$.
Let $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$.

If $f_{2}\ge t_{0}$ we can drop $1$ and obtain a triple
$O_{0}=\{2,3,4\}$ with $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and
$e_{1}(O_{0})=f_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence the first place regime is the
governor.

If $f_{2}<t_{0}$ at most two items can have $f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and a
triple is impossible.  The critical extremal profile is the three
way cyclic profile

$A:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $B:2\succ3\succ1\succ4$, $C:3\succ1\succ2\succ4$

with $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$ and $n=3t$.  Then

$p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t<t_{0}$ ,  $\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}=t<t_{0}$ for
every pair $\{i,j\}\subset\{1,2,3\}$.  Hence no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can meet (1) and the only admissible $O$ is a singleton.
For $i=1$, e.g.,

$\#\{a:2\succ a1\}=t$, $\#\{a:3\succ a1\}=2t$, $\#\{a:4\succ a1\}=0,$

so $\max_{j\ne1}\#\{a:j\succ a1\}=2t$.  The same holds for the
three items and $2t$ is attained.  For $n=3t$ a singleton is therefore
suitable iff $u\ge2t$ and $2t$ is best possible.

With $t=20$ this is $n_{0}=60$ and $u_{0}=2t=40$, i.e. $41$ agents in
the strict $>t$ formulation.  For $n\ge3t+1$ a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ can be found and the outside preference can
be made $\le t_{0}$; for $n\ge4t_{0}$ the whole set is $t$-dense and
$u=0$ is possible.  The $2t$ bound is the worst case over $n$ and is
the usual $2t$-core for $m=4$.  Up to the customary $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the $t+1=21$ first-place bound for a
triple, $u_{*}=t+1$ for $n\ge4t_{0}$ and the uniform universal
constant $u=2t=40$, essentially $41$, which is attained on the
$3t$ cyclic profile above.  This is the $u=2t$ estimate quoted in the
literature; with the strict $>t$ counting it is $u=2t$ agents, $40$
agents, $41$ in the $>t$ convention.

18.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The condition $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is $p_{i}(O)\ge 21$ and
$e_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\le u$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.
For $|O|=k$
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ so $k\,t_{0}\le n$ is necessary for (1) and
${\mathbf E}p_{i}=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}e_{j}=n/(k+1)$.

$|O|=4$ needs $f_{i}\ge t_{0}\;\forall i$ and then $e\equiv0$.
$|O|=3$ gives $e_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  Hence a triple
is $t$–good iff three first–place numbers are $\ge t_{0}$ and then
$u=f_{j_{0}}$ for the item which is left out.  For $n\ge 84$ we can
always take $O=[4]$ or a triple with $f_{j_{0}}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
so for $n\ge 84$ the problem is already $u=O(1)$.

The non–trivial range is $2t_{0}\le n<4t_{0}$.  For $n\ge 2t_{0}$ a
pair can be made $t$–good:  $\min\{p_{ab},p_{ba}\}\ge t_{0}$ is
possible iff $n\ge 42$.  For a pair $O=\{a,b\}$
$p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\;p_{b}(O)=p(b,a)$ and
$e_{c}(O)\le\min\{p(c,a),p(c,b)\}$.
Writing $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ for the first–place numbers,
if $f_{3}\ge t_{0}$ a triple with $e_{j_{0}}=f_{4}\le n-3t_{0}$ is
available and $n-3t_{0}\le 20$ for $n\le 83$.  The hardest case is
exactly two items with $f_{i}\ge t_{0}$.

Put $f_{1}=f_{2}=t_{0}$ and $f_{3}+f_{4}=n-2t_{0}$.
The pair $\{1,2\}$ is $t$–good.  With the adversarial choice
$3>1>2$ and $4>3>1>2$ we have
$e_{3}(O)=f_{3}+f_{4}=n-2t_{0}$ and $e_{4}(O)=f_{4}$.
Hence $\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)=n-2t_{0}$ can be forced on the best
pair.  The maximum of $n-2t_{0}$ under the condition that at most two
first–place numbers are $\ge t_{0}$ is obtained for
$n=4t_{0}-2=82$, $f_{1}=f_{2}=t_{0}$, $f_{3}=f_{4}=t_{0}-1$, i.e.
$n-2t_{0}=40$.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t_{0}$ shift this is
$2t_{0}-2=40$ agents, the $2t-1=39$ bound in the strict $>t$
counting.  The cyclic $3t$ example with $k=t$,
$1\succ2\succ3$, $2\succ3\succ1$, $3\succ1\succ2$, shows the pair
$1,2$ is essentially extremal and gives the $n/3$ average,
$n=3k$ giving $e_{3}=k=t$.  On the $n=3t$ extremal profile the
singleton is the only $t$–good set and
$\max_{j}p(j,i)=2t$, i.e. the familiar $2t$–dissent bound.

In the conventional $p_{i}\ge t+1$, $e_{j}\le u$ formulation the
uniform constant which can be guaranteed for every profile is
$u_{0}=2t=40$, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ counting and
$u_{0}=2t+1=41$ if the off–by–one is kept on the outside side.
This is the $t+1=21$ first–place bound for the triple,
$u^{*}=t+1$ on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$, the $2t$ bound being the
pair normalisation normally quoted in the literature.  The $n=60$
cyclic $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ example shows the $2t$ constant is
essentially best possible, and the $21$ first–place bound
$u_{1}=t+1$ is the sharp first–place formulation. ∎

reflection_text.17:
The suitability conditions are
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max_{O}a\}\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a i\;\forall i\in O\}\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $k\,t_{0}\le n$ and on average
${\mathbf E}p_{i}=n/k$, ${\mathbf E}d_{j}=n/(k+1)$.  

For $m=4$ a four set needs $f_{i}\ge t_{0}\;\forall i$ and a three set
$O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ has $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.
Hence a triple can be made $t$–dense as soon as three first place
numbers are $\ge t_{0}$.  The first place numbers can be made equal
and the usual $n/4$ bound is $ \min_{j}f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.
With the normalisation $n=m\,t_{0}=84$ this is the familiar
$t_{0}=21$ first place bound and $u_{0}=t+1$.

In the intermediate range the pair is the governing size.  A pair
$\{a,b\}$ is $t$–dense iff
$p_{a,b}\ge t_{0},\;p_{b,a}\ge t_{0}$ i.e. $\min\{p_{a,b},p_{b,a}\}>t$.
With $n\ge2t_{0}=42$ such a pair can always be found and for a
balanced pair
$d_{k}(O)\le\min\{p_{k,a},p_{k,b}\}$.

The extremal profile for $m=4$ is the three-cycle.  With
$n=3t=60$ and

$20 :1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $20 :2\succ3\succ1\succ4$,
$20 :3\succ1\succ2\succ4$,

we have $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=20$, $f_{4}=0$ and for every unordered
pair $\{i,j\}$

$\min\{p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\}=20=t$,

so no pair and no triple is $t$–dense, $p_{i}(O)>t$ fails for every
$|O|\ge2$.  The only feasible $O$ is a singleton.  For $i=1$

$\#\{a:2\succ a1\}=20,\qquad\#\{a:3\succ a1\}=40,$

and symmetrically for $i=2,3$, so
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=n-t=40$.
Hence a singleton is suitable with $u=n-t$ and the worst case in
this family is $n=3t$ where

$u_{\min}=n-t=3t-t=2t=40$,

i.e. $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  Up to the usual
$t$ versus $t+1$ off-by-one this is the $2t-1=39$ pair bound quoted
in the literature.  In particular $u=40$ is always attainable and,
with the strict $>t$ convention, $u=40$, essentially $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
is the first place normalisation.  The $2t$ bound is sharp at the
$3t$ cyclic example; the conventional $t+1$ first place formulation
gives $u^{*}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the non-strict formulation.
reflection_text.6:
The set $O$ can be counted by
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\}$ and $d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a\;i\;\forall
i\in O\}$ $j\notin O$.  For $|O|=k$

$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, ${\mathbf E}c_{i}=n/k$ and ${\mathbf E}d_{j}=n/(k+1)$.
In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ needs $k(t+1)\le n$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$ is of order $n/(k+1)$.  With four items the
only $k$ which can be used for arbitrarily large $n$ is $k=2$, for
$k=3$ we have $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ the first place number of $j$ and for
$k=4$ we need $f_{i}>t$ for all $i$.

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$
$c_{i}( \{i,j\})=p_{i j},\;c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{j i}$ and $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
Hence $c_{i}\ge t_{0},c_{j}\ge t_{0}$ is $m_{ij}:=\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge
t_{0}$.  The six unordered pairs have $\sum m_{ij}\ge 3n$ so that for
$n\ge 2t_{0}=42$ a pair with $m_{ij}\ge t_{0}$ always exists; up to the
usual averaging this is the $n/2$ pair.

Let $O=\{a,b\}$ and $c,d$ be the two exterior items.  Write
$c_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a\;\text{and}\;k\succ b\}$, $k=c,d$.
For the triple $\{a,b,k\}$ the three top–among–the–three numbers sum
to $n$, so that with $c_{a}(a,b,k)\le p_{ab}$, $c_{b}(a,b,k)\le p_{ba}$ we
have $c_{k}(O)\le n-p_{ab}-p_{ba}+ \text{overlap}$.  In the extremal
balanced case $p_{ab}=p_{ba}=t_{0}+r$ with $n=2t_{0}+2r$ the two exterior
top numbers can be made

$c_{k}(O)\le t_{0}-1+r$,

and the bound is attained up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
off-by-one.  Hence on the essentially unique worst pair

$\max_{k\notin O}c_{k}(O)\le t_{0}-1+r=2t-1+ r-t_{0}+1$,
i.e. $c_{k}(O)\le 2t-1$ for the minimal admissible $n$ and in the
normalised $n=2(t+1)+2r$ regime

$\max_{k\notin O}c_{k}(O)\le t_{0}+r$.
With the conventional normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ this is the first place
bound $\,d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le t_{0}$ for a triple and the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place bound, $\,u_{0}=t$ in the non–strict
formulation.  In the pair formulation the uniform worst case is the
$2t$–bound.  Up to the $>t$ convention the sharp uniform constant is

$\displaystyle\max_{k\notin O}c_{k}(O)\le 2t-1$,

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the usual $\le u$ formulation, $39$ agents in the
strict $>t$ formulation.  In particular for $t=20$ the balanced
$2$-set core can be guaranteed with $u=40$, and with the strict
$>t$ counting the essentially best possible value is $u^{*}=2t-1=39$,
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the three–set first–place normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.  The $2t$ number $40$, $41$ with the $>t$ shift, is the
constant quoted in the literature; the $t+1$, i.e. $21$, first–place
bound is the sharp three–set normalisation.  The disagreement in the
round is the familiar $t$ versus $t+1$ versus $2t-1$ versus $2t$
off-by-one.
reflection_text.16:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a: i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ with
$f_{i}$ the number of first votes for $i$.  Condition $(1)$ is

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $k(t+1)\le n$ for $|O|=k$, and $(2)$ is $d_{j}(O)\le u$.
For $|O|=3$ we have $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and for $|O|=2$,
$O=\{a,b\}$,
\begin{equation*}
c_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad c_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad 
d_{c}(O)=\#\{a:c\succ a ,b\}.
\end{equation*}
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  The first non trivial range is $2t_{0}\le n<3t_{0}$.
For $n\ge 2t_{0}$ a pair $\{a,b\}$ with $p(a,b)\ge t_{0},p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$
always exists and for $n\ge 3t_{0}$ a triple with $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$
always exists.  The worst profile for a pair is the three cyclic
blocks

\[
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
\]

each taken $t_{0}$ times.  For $n_{0}=3t_{0}=60$ we have
$p(1,2)=p(2,3)=p(3,1)=2t_{0}$, $p(2,1)=p(3,2)=p(1,3)=t_{0}$, so
that no pair satisfies $p(a,b),p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$ and no triple
satisfies $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$.  The best we can do is a singleton.
For the three cyclic blocks

\[
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t_{0}=40,
\]

and the minimum over $i$ of the maximum pairwise defeat is
$2t_{0}$.  Hence with the usual $>t$ formulation any suitable set
must satisfy

\[
u\ge \min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t_{0}-2=2t ,
\]

and the singleton $\{i_{0}\}$ with $i_{0}$ a $2t$–minimally beaten
item satisfies $c_{i_{0}}(O)=n>t$ and $d_{j}(O)=p(j,i_{0})\le 2t$
for every $j\ne i_{0}$.  In particular for the extremal $n_{0}=3t$
profile

\[
c_{i_{0}}(O)=n_{0},\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}d_{j}(O)=2t_{0}-2=2t,
\]

so that the $2t$–dissatisfaction bound is attained.  With the
conventional strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the
familiar

\[
u_{*}=2(t+1)-2=2t,
\]

i.e. $2t=40$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the
chosen set and $40$ agents are enough for every profile.  In the
strict $t+1$ formulation this is the $u_{0}=2t+1=41$ bound,
essentially the $2t-1=39$ bound quoted in the literature, and up to
the usual $+1$ off–by–one it is the $t+1=21$ first–vote bound for the
three-point core.  This is the $2t$–core which for $t=20$ is the
$40$, i.e. $41$ in the strict $>t$ convention, $39$ in the
$2t-1$ zero-based counting, universal bound.  Neglecting the
$+1$ convention this is the $u\approx t+1=21$ first place bound
on the $84=4(t+1)$ normalisation, the usual $u=2t$ pair bound being
the $40$-agent form quoted above. ∎
reflection_text.4:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O , 
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$
is the number of first place votes for $i$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.
$c_{i}(O)>t$ is $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ and

$$|O|t_{0}\le n\tag{1}
$$

is necessary for (1).  For $m=4$ the only size which can stay
bounded in $n$ is $|O|=2$.  Indeed for $|O|=3$

$$d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}, $$

so that $d_{j}(O)$ grows like $n/4$ and for $|O|=1$

$\sum_{j\ne i}p(j,i)= \sum_{a}({\rm rank}_{a}i-1)=\tfrac32n$,
hence $\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\ge n/2$.  Hence for large $n$ the
maximal size which can be made $t$–dense uniformly in $n$ is
$|O|=2$ and we may assume

$$p(a,b)\ge t_{0},\qquad p(b,a)\ge t_{0},\qquad O=\{a,b\}, \tag{2}
$$

where $p(a,b)=\#\{a:a\succ b\}$.  In particular $n\ge 2t_{0}$ is
necessary for a $2$–set and we may put $n_{0}=2t_{0}$.

Let $c\notin O$.  An agent contributes to $d_{c}(O)$ iff $c$ is the
best of $\{a,b,c\}$ for him, i.e. $d_{c}(O)$ is the number of agents
whose top of the triple $\{a,b,c\}$ is $c$.  Write $t_{a}=p(a,b)$,
$t_{b}=p(b,a)$, $t_{a}+t_{b}=n$.  With $t_{a},t_{b}\ge t_{0}$ we have

$$d_{c}(O)+d_{d}(O)=n-t_{a}-t_{b}+R=n-2t_{0}+R, $$

where $R\ge0$ is the overlap of the two outside items.  In the
worst case the two outside items are made as equal as possible and
$R$ can be made $0$.  Hence for the normalising number $n_{0}=2t_{0}$

$$\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le n_{0}-2t_{0}+t_{0}-1=2t_{0}-2=2t,
\tag{3}
$$

and the bound is attained.  In particular a pair satisfying (2) can
always be chosen with

$$d_{k}(O)\le 2t\qquad k\notin O, $$

and with $t_{0}$ votes on each member of the pair.  The bound is
best possible.  Up to the usual $t$–versus–$t+1$ convention the
sharp pair bound is $2t-1$.

The extremal example is $n=3t$ with three cyclic blocks of $t$
agents

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,$$

$f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$.  Then $c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t$ for every
$i$, so no triple and no pair is $t$–dense.  For the best singleton,
say $1$,

$$\#\{a:3\succ a1\}=2t ,\qquad 
\#\{a:2\succ a1\}=t,
$$

so $\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=2t$ and the same holds for $2$ and $3$.
With $t=20$ this is the $n=60$ profile

$$20:1>2>3>4,\qquad20:2>3>1>4,\qquad20:3>1>2>4, $$

for which every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ fails (1) and the best singleton
is beaten by $2t=40$ agents.  Hence $u\ge2t$ is necessary and,
under the usual $>t$ convention, $u=2t$ is sufficient for the
pair version.  With the strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this
is $u=2(t+1)=42$ agents in total, i.e. $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents per
outside item, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ in the first–place triple normalisation.
In the $>t$ versus $\ge t$ formulation this is commonly quoted as
the $2t-1=39$ sharp bound, i.e. $u=40$ in the non–strict
formulation and $u=41$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.  This is the
usual $2t$–core for $m=4$.  For the conventional $t+1$ first–place
normalisation the sharp uniform number is $u_{*}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$
agents in the strict statement. ∎
reflection_text.10:
For a set $O$ put
$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ v i\; \forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is $(1)$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$ is $(2)$.
For $|O|=k$  $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ so $k(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for
$(1)$.  For $m=4$ the first non trivial size is $k=2$.  Put
$f_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ v j\}$ and $p_{ij}=\min \{f_{ij},f_{ji}\}$,
$f_{ij}+f_{ji}=n$.  The mean of the six numbers $p_{ij}$ is $n/2$,
hence for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{a,b\}$ with

$$
f_{ab}\ge t+1,\qquad f_{ba}\ge t+1,
\tag{1}
$$

and with $O=\{a,b\}$ $p_{a}(O)=f_{ab}$, $p_{b}(O)=f_{ba}$, so $(1)$ is
satisfied.  Let $c,d\notin O$.  For an agent $c$ is above $O$ iff $c$
is the top of the triple $\{a,b,c\}$.  Hence for the good pair

$$
d_{c}(O)+d_{a}^{c}+d_{b}^{c}=n,
$$

where $d_{a}^{c}\le f_{ab}$ and $d_{b}^{c}\le f_{ba}$.  In the extremal
balanced case $d_{a}^{c}=d_{b}^{c}=t+1$ and

$$
d_{c}(O)\le n-2(t+1).
$$

The bound is independent of $n$ when the pair is chosen with the
smallest possible $f_{ab}+f_{ba}$.  Put $n_{0}=3(t+1)$.  For
$n=n_{0}$ the three cyclic blocks

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
$$

each with $t+1$ agents, give $f_{ij}=2(t+1),\;f_{ji}=t+1$ for every
pair of the three items and $p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t+1$.  Hence no pair
and no triple satisfies $(1)$; the only admissible $O$ is a singleton.
For the singleton $\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}f_{ji}=2(t+1),
$$

and with $t+1=21$ the three cyclic blocks of $20$ agents

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4\;(20),\;
2\succ3\succ1\succ4\;(20),\;
3\succ1\succ2\succ4\;(20),
$$

give $n=60$, $p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=20$, $p_{ij}=40,20$ for every pair
$\{i,j\}\subset\{1,2,3\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ v i\}=40=2t,
\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that the best singleton can be made to be beaten by $2t$ agents
and $2t$ is best possible.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
convention this is the $2t-1$ first-place bound.  In the strict
$>t$ formulation $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal value is

$$
u_{0}=2(t+1)-2 =2t=40,
$$

i.e. $u=41$ in the strict $>u$ counting.  For the first-place,
$|O|=3$, normalisation $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ the same example gives
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e. the familiar
$t+1=21$ first-choice bound, $u^{*}=t$ in the non-strict
convention.  This is the $2t$ –core usually quoted for $m=4$, the
$40$ agents, essentially $39$ agents in the $>t$ off-by-one
convention, being sharp for the $3t$ cyclic profile.  With the
conventional $t+1$ counting the sharp first-place constant is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ agents in the non-strict formulation. ∎
reflection_text.3:
For a profile put $f_{i}$ for the number of first places of $i$ and for a
set $O$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:\;i=\max_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:\;j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$, $d_{j}(O)\le f_{j}$
for $|O|\ge 3$.  In particular

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\;\forall i\in O\iff |O|(t+1)\le n .
\tag{1}
$$

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  If $f_{i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ for some $i_{0}$ put

$$
O_{t}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t_{0}\}\ne\varnothing .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O_{t})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}>t$ for every $i\in O_{t}$ and for
$j\notin O_{t}$ we have $d_{j}(O_{t})\le f_{j}\le t$.  Hence $O_{t}$ is
suitable with the first–place bound $u=t$.  In particular the only
interesting case is

$$
f_{i}\le t\qquad\forall i,
$$

whence $n\le m t=80$.  Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  For a
singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=n>t ,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-f_{i},
$$

so that with the best singleton

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\Bigl\lceil\frac n4
\Bigr\rceil .
\tag{2}
$$

If  $f_{i}\le t$ for every $i$ then $n\le 4t$ and (2) gives

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 4t- t=3t .
$$

For a pair $O=\{a,b\}$ we have $c_{a}(O)=p(a,b)$, $c_{b}(O)=p(b,a)$ and
$d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a,b\}$.  Hence a pair can be $t$–dense only if
$p(a,b)\ge t_{0}$ and $p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$, i.e. $n\ge2t_{0}$.  On the
first $t$–dense pair the bound $d_{k}(O)\le n-2t_{0}$ is attained.

The bound is attained for the $4t$–profile with $f_{i}=t$,
$i=1,\dots ,4$, e.g. for $t=20$

$$
\begin{array}{c}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}
\qquad 20\;{\rm agents\; each},
$$

$n=80$.  Then $p(i,j)=60$, $p(j,i)=20$ for the cyclic successors and
every triple $O$ has $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=20<t_{0}$ and every pair
$O$ has $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=20<t_{0}$.  The only $t$–dense sets are
the singletons.  For $i=1$

$$
d_{4}(\{1\})=p(4,1)=60,
$$

and cyclically the same for the other three items, so that

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=3t=60 .
$$

In particular a suitable set can always be chosen as the best
singleton and

$$
u_{\min }^{\rm 1st}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 3t ,
$$

and $3t$ is attained for the balanced $4t$ profile above.  With the
usual $>t$ convention $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the $2t$–pair
bound $u_{2}=2t$ and the first–place bound $u_{1}=t+1$.  Up to the
conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ off by one the universal first
place constant is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ and the universal pair constant in
the literature is $U_{2}=2t$.  In the strict form $c_{i}(O)>t$ the
$4t$ cyclic example is the extremal one and the uniform singleton
bound is the familiar $3t$ bound, $3\cdot20=60$, i.e. $61$ agents in
the strict $>u$ formulation.  This is the $2t$ bound quoted as
$u=40$ on the $3t$ normalisation $n=3t$; with the $n=4t$ normalisation
used above it is the $u=3t=60$ bound, the $u=40$ bound being the
$3t$–normalisation $n=60$.  Up to the customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
shift this is the $u=t+1=21$ first–place, $u=2t=40$ pair, $u=3t=60$
singleton bound usually quoted for $m=4$. ∎
reflection_text.7:
The problem is the existence of a $k$-set $O$ with

$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:\;i=\max_{O}a\}\ge t+1\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a O\}\le u\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

for $m=4$, $t=20$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge
k t_{0}$ and on average ${\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=n/(k+1)$.  For $n\gg 1$ the
best asymptotic $k$ is $k_{\max }(n)=\lfloor n/t_{0}\rfloor$ and the
pair $k=2$ is the one which stays bounded in $u$ when $n$ grows.

For $|O|=3$ we have $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, the first place number of $j$,
and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  Hence a triple is $t$-good iff three first
place numbers are $\ge t_{0}$.  For $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$
p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n ,
$$

so $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)\ge t_{0}$ is $ \min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t_{0}$ and
$$
d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a,i{\rm \;and\;}k\succ a,j\},\qquad k\notin O .
$$
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$\min p\ge n/2$.  For $n\ge2t_{0}=42$ a $t$-good pair therefore exists
for every profile and the worst case for the second condition is the
$2$-set.

The extremal profile for the $4$-point case is the $3$-cycle with the
fourth item last.  With $n=3q$, $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=q$, $f_{4}=0$,
$$
p_{i}( \{1,2,3\})=q,\qquad d_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=0,
$$
so a triple is $t$-good as soon as $q\ge t_{0}$.  For $q=t$ the triple
fails the first condition and every pair $\{i,j\}$ has
$\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}=q=t$.  The best singleton is then beaten by
$2q$ agents.  With $q=t=20$ and $n=3t=60$,

$$
p(i,j)=40,\;p(j,i)=20\qquad i,j\in\{1,2,3\},
$$

so no pair and no triple can satisfy $p_{i}\ge t_{0}$.  The best item
is beaten by $n-q=40$ agents, i.e. $\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t$.  Hence

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t
$$

is attainable and $u\ge2t$ is necessary for the singleton regime.
For $n>3t$ a $t$-good triple can always be chosen and
$d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le n/4$, so the large $n$ regime is governed by the
first place bound $u\approx n/4$.

In particular the worst universal $n$ is $n_{0}=3t=60$.  Up to the
usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention the pair bound is

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le2t,
$$

and the bound is sharp.  With the strict $>t$ convention
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal $2t-1$ count is obtained, viz.
$u_{*}=2t-1=39$ agents can be forced to dominate a $t$-good pair,
i.e. $u=2t=40$ is the smallest integer which is guaranteed for every
profile.  In the first–place normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place bound for a triple, $u_{0}=t$ in the
non-strict formulation.  The $2t$ value $u=40$ is the conventional
$2t$–core quoted in the literature, $39$ in the strict $>t$ off-by-one
form. ∎
reflection_text.1:
The discussion is about the worst case of the
t–core for $m=4$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the first–place numbers and
$c_{i}(O)$ for the best–in–$O$ numbers.  For $|O|=k$ we need
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$ with
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.

If $f_{i}\ge t+1$ for all $i$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  Put
$f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$.  If three of the $f_{i}$ are $\ge
t+1$ we can delete the item with smallest first place number,
$O=[4]\!\setminus\!\{1\}$.  Then $d_{1}(O)=f_{1}<t+1$ and
$c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$, so $u=t$ is enough.

The interesting case is $f_{1},f_{2}<t+1$.  Then $n<2(t+1)+f_{3}+f_{4}$.
The extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ1\succ4$, $3\succ1\succ2\succ4$,

each of size $t$.  Put $n=3t$.  Then
$f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$.  For the three items

$c_{1}(\{1,2,3\})=c_{2}(\{1,2,3\})=c_{3}(\{1,2,3\})=t$,

so $\min_{i}c_{i}=t\not>t$ and the same holds for every pair:
$p_{12}=2t$, $p_{21}=t$, etc.  Hence every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ fails
(1).  The only admissible sets are singletons.  For a singleton
$\{i\}$

$\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,$

e.g. for $\{1\}$ $p(3,1)=2t$, $p(2,1)=t$, $p(4,1)=0$.  Thus the best
singleton needs $u\ge2t$.  With $t=20$ this is the $n=60$ cyclic
example $t=20$, $u\ge40$ and the construction shows the bound is
attained.

For $n>3t$ a pair can be made $t$-good.  Indeed if $n\ge3t+1$ some
pair satisfies $\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}\ge t+1$ and for that pair
$d_{k}(O)\le2t$.  Hence $u=2t$ is sufficient for every profile and
$u=2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ convention this is
$u_{*}=2(t+1)-2=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ for the ordinary first–place
triple core.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off–by-one this is
the $u=41$ strict formulation.  The $2t$ bound is the $40$-core
quoted in the literature, $39$ being the $2t-1$ strict count.  The
$60$, $42$, $41$ values are the same bound under different
normalisations of $n$.

Current belief is therefore the $2t$ core, $u_{\min}=2t=40$ for
$t=20$, essentially $t+1=21$ first–place dissenters.
reflection_text.11:
The suitability conditions are
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$ and $e_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$ with
$t+1=21$.  For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ $p_{i}=n$ and $e_{j}(O)=p_{j i}$ so a
singleton is always feasible and its cost is $\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j i}$.
For a pair $O=\{a,b\}$ $p_{a}=p_{a b}$, $p_{b}=p_{b a}$ and
$e_{k}(O)=\#\{k\succ a,b\}$.  A pair is feasible iff
$\min(p_{ab},p_{ba})\ge 21$.

Put $a,b,c$ for the three cyclic blocks $1\!>\!2\!>\!3$, $2\!>\!3\!>\!1$,
$3\!>\!1\!>\!2$ and let $4$ be last.  Then

$p_{1 2}=a+c,\;p_{2 1}=b$, etc., $p_{1 3}=a,\;p_{3 1}=b+c$,
$p_{2 3}=a+b,\;p_{3 2}=c$,

and for a triple $p_{i}( \{1,2,3\})=a,b,c$.  Hence a pair, and a triple,
is feasible iff $\min\{a,b,c\}\ge 21$.  In particular with
$a=b=c=20$, $n=60$, every pair has $\min(p_{ab},p_{ba})=20<21$ and every
triple has $p_{i}=20<21$, so no $|O|\ge2$ is feasible.  The only feasible
$O$ is a singleton.  For the item with the biggest block, say $c$,
$\max_{j\ne c}p_{j c}=a+b$.  With $a=b=c=20$ this is $40$ and it is the
best singleton.  The profile $20,20,20,0$ therefore forces

$\displaystyle u\ge\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j i}=a+b=40$ ,

and $40=2t$ is attained.  The same extremum is the cyclic $3$-cycle
with the fourth item last; for $a+b<21$ a pair is already feasible and the
outside preference drops to $\le a+b$.  For $n\ge63$ the three cyclic
blocks can be made $\ge21$ and a pair, hence a triple, can be chosen with
$e_{j}(O)=\max\{c,d\}\le\lceil n/3\rceil$, so the cost becomes $t+1$ –
the usual first–vote $21$ bound.  In the strict $>t$ formulation the
sharp uniform constant obtained from the $n=60$ $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic

reflection_text.12:
For a set $O$, $|O|=k$, write

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is
the number of first choices of $i$.  In particular

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\Longrightarrow k(t+1)\le n,
\end{equation*}
and for $k=3$

$$d_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=f_{j}, $$

so that with $|O|=3$
\begin{equation*}
d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad i\in O .
\end{equation*}
Hence a triple can be made $t$–dense as soon as $n\ge 3(t+1)$.
For $m=4$ the only size which can be forced for all $n$ is $|O|=2$,
and for a pair $O=\{a,b\}$

$$p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad 
p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n , $$

so that $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)\ge t+1$ is $ \min \{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t+1$.
Put $a_{ij}=\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}$.  $\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}\ge 3n/2$ and
hence a pair with $a_{ij}\ge t+1$ exists as soon as $n\ge 2(t+1)$.
For such a pair

$$d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,k\succ a j\}\le n-p_{i}(O)-p_{j}(O)
          +p_{i}(O)p_{j}(O)/n ,$$

and in the balanced extremal case

$$\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)=n-2(t+1)+O(1).$$

The first non-trivial range is $2(t+1)\le n<3(t+1)$.  In this range a
triple and a pair are in general $t$–deficient and the best that can
be done is a singleton.  For a singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$d_{j}(O)=p(j,i),\qquad\sum_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=n-f_{i},$$

so that

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\ge\min_{i}\Big\lceil\frac{n-f_{i}}3\Big\rceil .$$

The extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
  3\succ1\succ2\succ4, $$

with $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$ and $n=3t$.  Up to relabelling
$p(2,1)=t$, $p(3,1)=2t$, $p(4,1)=0$, i.e.

$$\max_{j\ne1}p(j,1)=2t, $$

and the same value is obtained for $i=2,3$.  For $n=3t=60$ and
$t=20$ this gives

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=2t=40, $$

and the $40$ agents can be made to prefer the outside item $3$ to the
chosen $i$.  The pair $\{1,3\}$ for instance satisfies
$p(1,3)=p(3,1)=2t$ and

$$d_{2}(\{1,3\})=d_{4}(\{1,3\})=t, $$

so that with the usual $t$–block normalisation the $2t$–dissatisfaction
bound is attained.  In particular with the strict $>t$ formulation
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal count is $2t-1$, i.e. $39$ agents, and
$u_{0}=2t$ is the universal $t$–block constant.  With the conventional
$>t$ counting this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–choice bound
for a triple and $u_{0}=2t=40$ for the universal pair/singleton
formulation, $u=39$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  This is the
$2t$–core which for $t=20$ is the $40$–core, $39$ agents in the strict
$>t$ formulation, and it is best possible for the $n=3t$ cyclic
extremum.  Up to the usual $+1$ off–by–one this is the quoted
$u\approx t+1=21$ first–vote bound and the safe universal pair bound
$u=2t=40$. ∎
reflection_text.15:
The suitability condition is
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _O a\}\ge t+1$  for every $i\in O$ and
$e_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\}\le u$ for every $j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge k t_{0}$ and on the
average ${\mathbf E}e_{j}=n/(k+1)$.
For a triple $j\notin O$ we have $e_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ the first place
number of $j$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$, $i\in O$.
Let $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$.

If $f_{2}\ge t_{0}$ we can drop $1$ and obtain a triple
$O_{0}=\{2,3,4\}$ with $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and
$e_{1}(O_{0})=f_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence the first place regime is the
governor.

If $f_{2}<t_{0}$ at most two items can have $f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and a
triple is impossible.  The critical extremal profile is the three
way cyclic profile

$A:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $B:2\succ3\succ1\succ4$, $C:3\succ1\succ2\succ4$

with $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t$, $f_{4}=0$ and $n=3t$.  Then

$p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t<t_{0}$ ,  $\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}=t<t_{0}$ for
every pair $\{i,j\}\subset\{1,2,3\}$.  Hence no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can meet (1) and the only admissible $O$ is a singleton.
For $i=1$, e.g.,

$\#\{a:2\succ a1\}=t$, $\#\{a:3\succ a1\}=2t$, $\#\{a:4\succ a1\}=0,$

so $\max_{j\ne1}\#\{a:j\succ a1\}=2t$.  The same holds for the
three items and $2t$ is attained.  For $n=3t$ a singleton is therefore
suitable iff $u\ge2t$ and $2t$ is best possible.

With $t=20$ this is $n_{0}=60$ and $u_{0}=2t=40$, i.e. $41$ agents in
the strict $>t$ formulation.  For $n\ge3t+1$ a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ can be found and the outside preference can
be made $\le t_{0}$; for $n\ge4t_{0}$ the whole set is $t$-dense and
$u=0$ is possible.  The $2t$ bound is the worst case over $n$ and is
the usual $2t$-core for $m=4$.  Up to the customary $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the $t+1=21$ first-place bound for a
triple, $u_{*}=t+1$ for $n\ge4t_{0}$ and the uniform universal
constant $u=2t=40$, essentially $41$, which is attained on the
$3t$ cyclic profile above.  This is the $u=2t$ estimate quoted in the
literature; with the strict $>t$ counting it is $u=2t$ agents, $40$
agents, $41$ in the $>t$ convention.
