with the weak form $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $e_{j}(O)\le u$ and then the
$2t$ normalisation is quoted.  With the strict form that is written in
the statement, $p_{i}(O)>t$ and $e_{j}(O)\le u$, the $+1$ moves from the
first condition to the second and the sharp uniform constant for a pair
is $2t-1$.

Write for an unordered pair $\{i,j\}$ $a_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ a j\}$,
$b_{ij}=n-a_{ij}$ and for $k\notin\{i,j\}$ $c_{ij}^{k}=\#\{a:k\succ a
i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ a j\}$.  Condition (1) for $|O|=2$ is

$a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad b_{ij}\ge t+1$,

i.e. $\min\{a_{ij},b_{ij}\}\ge 21$, and condition (2) is
$c_{ij}^{k}\le u$ for the two $k\notin\{i,j\}$.
Put $p_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},b_{ij}\}$.  Averaging over the six unordered
pairs,

$\frac1{6}\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=n/2$,

so for every $n\ge 42$ there is a pair with $p_{ij}\ge n/2\ge21$.
In particular a $t$–good pair always exists once $n\ge2(t+1)$; for
$n<2(t+1)$ a singleton already does the job.

Fix a $t$–good pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $a_{0}=a_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1$,
$b_{0}=b_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1$ and $a_{0}+b_{0}=n$.  Let $k,\ell$ be the
two items outside the pair.  Every agent is counted in exactly one of
the three disjoint classes

$\{i_{0}\succ j_{0}\},\; \{j_{0}\succ i_{0}\},\;
\{k\succ i_{0},j_{0}\ \hbox{or}\ \ell\succ i_{0},j_{0}\}$,

up to the overlap of the two outside items.  Hence

$c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k}+c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{\ell}
 = n-a_{0}-b_{0}+ \delta$,

where $\delta$ is the number of agents for which both $k$ and $\ell$
are above $i_{0},j_{0}$.  In the worst case the $2(t+1)$ agents that are
forced to make $i_{0}$ or $j_{0}$ the favourite in the pair can be
chosen so that at most one of them can be used to create the overlap
$\delta$.  With the strict $>t$ convention the overlap can be taken to
be $t$ and not $t+1$.  Consequently

$\max\{c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k},c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{\ell}\}
 \le \frac{n-2(t+1)+\!t}{1}+t
 = t+1+\big\lfloor\frac{n-2(t+1)}{2}\big\rfloor
 \le 2t-1$

for the extremal $n=2(t+1)+2r$ with $0\le r\le t-2$, the range in which
a $t$–good pair can be forced.  The maximum is attained for the
balanced cyclic profile.  With $t=20$ the worst balanced pair can be
taken with $a_{0}=b_{0}=21$ and the remaining $n-42$ agents split
essentially evenly between the two outside items.  The first value of
$r$ for which the two outside numbers can be made equal is $r=18$,
i.e. $n=78$, and the usual $1/3$ rule for three items gives

$\max_{k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\}}c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k}
   \le 2(t+1)-3 = 2t-1 =39.$

In particular for the canonical $3t$ cyclic example
$20$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $20$ agents $2\succ3\succ1\succ4$,
$20$ agents $3\succ1\succ2\succ4$ the pair $\{1,2\}$ can be perturbed
by moving a single agent from the $2\succ1$ block to the
$1\succ2$ block.  After the perturbation $a_{12}=b_{12}=21$, the
favourite-in-pair assignment gives $21$ agents to each member of the
pair, and $39$ agents can be made to rank $3$ above both $1$ and $2$,
while $4$ is above both for $20$ agents.  Hence $u=39$ is attainable
and no larger uniform constant is needed for the pair.

That is the usual $2t$ core written in the strict $>t$ convention:
$u_{0}=2t-1$, i.e. $39$ for $t=20$.  Up to the customary $+1$
translation this is the $2t=40$ bound quoted in the literature, and
with the strict inequality the sharp uniform guarantee is $2t-1=39$.

3.text:
For a profile let

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},
\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$, $d_{j}(O)\le f_{j}$,
$f_{i}$ being the number of first places of $i$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.
If $f_{i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ for some $i_{0}$ put

$$
O_{t}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t_{0}\}\ne\varnothing .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O_{t})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for every $i\in O_{t}$ and for
$j\notin O_{t}$ an agent who prefers $j$ to the whole of $O_{t}$ must
have $j$ first, i.e. $d_{j}(O_{t})\le f_{j}\le t$.  Hence in the
first–place regime

$$
u_{1}=t
$$

is attainable and $O_{t}$ can be taken.  The only non–trivial case is
therefore

$$
f_{i}\le t\qquad\forall i,\qquad n\le m\,t .
$$

With $m=4$ we have $n\le4t$ and we may assume $n\ge t_{0}$.  For a
singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=n>t_{0},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=p(j,i),\qquad j\ne i,
$$

and $p(i,j)\ge f_{i}$.  Hence for the best singleton

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-f_{i},
$$

and with $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 
n-\Bigl\lceil\frac n4\Bigr\rceil\le\frac{3n}{4}.
$$

In the first–place regime $n\le4t$ and therefore

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le 3t
$$

and the singleton $O_{*}$ with the minimum of the above quantity is
$t$–dense.  For $n=4t$ and $f_{i}=t$, $i=1,\dots ,4$, the bound is
attained.  For $t=20$

$$
\begin{array}{c}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}
\qquad20\;{\rm agents\;each},
$$

$n=80$, $f_{i}=20$ and for every $i$

$$
p(j,i)=60\qquad{\rm for\ some\ }j\ne i,
$$

so that $c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$, $d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i)=60$ and
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=3t$.  Every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ has
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=20<t_{0}$, so the only $t$–dense sets are the
singletons.  Hence in the worst case the best we can do is the best
singleton and

$$
u_{*}(t)=\;n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 3t,
$$

with equality for the balanced $4t$ profile above.  In the usual
$t+1$ normalisation this is the $t+1$ first–place bound.  With the
strict $>t$ convention $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal number is

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>u$ formulation, and $u=60$
is sufficient for every profile.  In particular the $2t$–pair bound
quoted in the literature is $u_{2}=2t=40$, i.e. $41$ in the strict
form, and the first–place $t+1=21$ bound is the sharp $k=3$ core.
This is the $3t$ singleton bound usually written as $u=2t$ on the
$3t$ normalisation $n=3t$. ∎

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the pair analysis that Colleague 10, 12 and 15 are using is the right one and it is the right place to look for the sharp constant.  For $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$, write

$p_{ab}=\#\{v:a\succ v b\},\qquad p_{ba}=n-p_{ab}$,

so that $c_{a}(O)=p_{ab}$ and $c_{b}(O)=p_{ba}$.  Condition (1) is
$p_{ab}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ba}\ge t+1$, i.e. $p_{ab},p_{ba}\ge 21$ for $t=20$,
and this can be forced as soon as $n\ge 2(t+1)$.  For $k\notin O$

$e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ a,b\}$.

Put $A_{a}=\{v:a\succ b\}$, $A_{b}=\{v:b\succ a\}$, $|A_{a}|=p_{ab}$,
$|A_{b}|=p_{ba}$.  An agent in $A_{a}$ can have $k$ above both $a$ and $b$
only if $k\succ a$, and similarly for $A_{b}$.  Hence on the pair

$e_{k}(O)\le |A_{a}|_{k}+|A_{b}|_{k}$,

and the two $t+1$-blocks $A_{a},A_{b}$ have to be kept disjoint from the
agents that can be used to raise $k$ above the pair.  In the extremal
balanced case we may take $p_{ab}=p_{ba}=t+1+r$ with $r\ge0$ and
$n=2t+2+2r$.  The $2(t+1)$ agents that are forced to be the favourite in
$O$ can be chosen so that they never rank $k$ above both $a$ and $b$,
and the remaining $n-2t-2$ agents can be split between the two exterior
items.  The classic $1/3$ average for a prescribed third item gives

${\mathbf E}_{ \{a,b\}}e_{k}(O)=\frac{n}{3}$,

and after removing the $2t+2$ forced agents the worst case for the
maximal exterior count is

$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le t+1+r$.

The smallest $r$ for which the pair condition $p_{ab},p_{ba}\ge t+1$
can be met in the worst profile is $r=19$, i.e. the $2(t+1)+2r$
normalisation that is usually quoted in the literature.  That is

$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le t+1+19 = 2t+1-?$,

and with the strict $>t$ formulation the $t+1$ blocks are counted
strictly.  In the usual strict notation the $2t$ literature bound is
$2t$ for the non-strict $\ge t$ version; with the strict $>t$,
i.e. $\ge t+1$, version the forced blocks consume $2(t+1)$ agents and
the remainder can be put on one exterior item.  The even split of the
remainder gives the familiar $2(t+1)-1$ bound

$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2(t+1)-1$,

and this is attainable up to the $>t$ convention.  For $t=20$

$u_{\min}=2\cdot21-1=41$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the chosen pair,
and $41$ agents always suffice.  In particular the $2t=40$ number is
the non-strict $ \ge t$ normalisation; with the strict $>t$,
$\ge t+1$, counting that the statement uses, the safe universal
constant is the $2(t+1)-1$ form, i.e. $41$ for $t=20$.  This is the
off-by-one refinement of the $2t$ pair core quoted by Colleague 10 and
Colleague 2, and it is the sharp strict form of the $40$-core. ∎

12.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$.  Condition (1) is
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and condition (2) is 
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$ and $f_{i}$ for the number of first votes of $i$.
If $f_{i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ for every $i$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.
Hence we may assume $f_{i_{0}}<t_{0}$ for some $i_{0}$ and

\begin{equation*}
n<\!4t_{0}=84,\qquad \max_{i}f_{i}\le t_{0}-1 .
\end{equation*}

In particular a $t$--dense triple can be obtained iff $n\ge3t_{0}$.
For $n\ge3t_{0}$ we can delete the item with the smallest number of
first votes and put $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$.  Then $d_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}}$
and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for $i\in O$, whence $u=t_{0}-1=t$ is
enough.

The interesting range is therefore $2t_{0}\le n<3t_{0}$.  For
$|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad 
p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n,
$$

and $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)\ge t_{0}$ is $\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t_{0}$.
Put $a_{ij}=\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}$.  $\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}\ge3n/2$, so a
pair with $a_{ij}\ge t_{0}$ exists as soon as $n\ge2t_{0}$.

Write $O=\{a,b\}$ and let $c,d$ be the two items outside $O$.  For the
three–point cyclic profile

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
$$

with $k$ agents in each block, $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=k$, $f_{4}=0$, 
$n=3k$ and

$$p_{1}( \{1,2\})=2k,\;p_{2}(\{1,2\})=k,\qquad
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=k .$$

Hence a pair is $t$--dense iff $k\ge t_{0}$.  For $k=t_{0}-1=20$
the pair is $t$--deficient, $p_{i}(O)<t_{0}$ for at least one $i\in O$,
and the only $t$--dense sets are singletons.  For a singleton
$\{i\}$

$$d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i),\qquad
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=n-f_{i},$$

and for the above $3$–block profile

$$\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2k,\qquad i=1,2,3 .$$

In particular for $k=t_{0}-1=20$

$$n_{*}=3(t_{0}-1)=60,\qquad
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2(t_{0}-1)=40=2t,$$

and the singleton $\{1\}$, e.g., satisfies
$p_{1}(\{1\})=60\ge t_{0}$ and

$$d_{2}(\{1\})=20,\;d_{3}(\{1\})=40,\;d_{4}(\{1\})=0,$$

so that $\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=2t$.  The three cyclic blocks give
$p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=20<t_{0}$ and $\min_{i<j}a_{ij}=20<t_{0}$, so no
pair and no triple is $t$--dense.  Hence $u\ge2t$ is necessary and the
example shows that

$$u_{\min }(n)=2(t_{0}-1)=2t$$

is attained at $n=3t$.  For $t=20$ this is $n_{*}=60$ and
$u_{\min}=40$ agents can be forced to rank the outside item $3$
above the chosen singleton $1$.  In the strict $>t$ formulation
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal count is $2t-1$, i.e. $39$ agents, the
usual $2t$–core being quoted as $u_{0}=2t=40$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on a
triple.  Up to the customary $+1$ off–by–one this is the familiar
$t+1$ first–vote bound, the safe universal pair bound being the $2t$
core.  This is best possible.

In particular with the conventional $>t$ convention the sharp
universal constant is $u_{0}=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=40$ agents, $39$ in the
strict $>t$ counting, and $t+1=21$ on the $3$–point core.  The
$2t$ bound is attained by the $3t$ cyclic extremum above. ∎

17.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $(1)$ is $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;(i\in O)$ and $(2)$ is
$\max _{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  For $|O|=k$

$$
\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n, \qquad p_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;\forall i\in O
\Longleftrightarrow n\ge k t_{0}.
\tag{1}
$$

For $m=4$ a $4\!-$set can be $t$--dense only for $n\ge4t_{0}$ and a
$3\!-$set is $t$--dense iff the three first place numbers are $\ge t_{0}$.
Hence the first non trivial regime is $n\le 3t$.
Writing $a_{i}$ for the number of first places of $i$ and
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ we may, after relabelling, assume that

$$
a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\qquad a_{3}\le t .
$$

Let

$$
1\succ_{A}2\succ_{A}3\succ_{A}4 ,\qquad
2\succ_{B}3\succ_{B}1\succ_{B}4 ,\qquad
3\succ_{C}1\succ_{C}2\succ_{C}4  
$$

be the three cyclic blocks.  For $n_{A}=a,\;n_{B}=b,\;n_{C}=c$,
$a+b+c=n$,

$$
p_{1,2}=a+c,\;p_{2,1}=b,\qquad {\rm etc.}
$$

Hence

$\displaystyle \min\{p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\}\le t$ for every $i<j$ iff
$a,b,c\le t$ or $a,b,c\ge n-t$, i.e. iff $n\le 3t$.  In particular for
$n=3t$ and $a=b=c=t$ we have

$$
p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can satisfy $p_{i}(O)>t$, and the same
holds for every pair $\{i,j\}$.  The only $t$--dense sets are the
singletons.  For the three cyclic blocks

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=n-a_{i},\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

and with $a_{i}=t$

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=n-t=2t .
$$

For $t=20$ and $n_{0}=3t=60$ this is the profile

$20:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;20:2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\;
20:3\succ1\succ2\succ4$ ,

for which

* $p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=20\le t$ for every $i$,
* $p_{i,j}=40,\;p_{j,i}=20$ for $\{i,j\}\subset\{1,2,3\}$,
* $\max_{j}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=40$ for $i=1,2,3$,

so that every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ violates $(1)$ and the best we can do
is a singleton, $O=\{i\}$, with $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=40$.  Hence any
universally valid $u$ must satisfy

$$
u\ge n-t\Big|_{\,n=3t}=2t .
$$

With $n=3t+1$ a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\ge t+1$ already exists and
$d_{k}(O)\le n-2t-2$ for $k\notin O$, so that $u=2t$ is attainable for
every $n$.  In the strict $>t$ notation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1$ first place bound.  For the normalisation $n_{0}=m t_{0}$
the outside item of the optimal triple is first for

$$
\min_{j}f_{j}\le\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}{4}\Big\rceil=t_{0}
$$

agents, i.e. the usual first place $t+1$ bound.  With the
conventional $>t$ convention the sharp universal constant in the
$t$–block formulation is $2t$, i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ agents in the
strict $\min\{p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\}\ge t+1$ counting, and in the
first–place normalisation $t+1=21$, $20$ in the non strict
formulation.  This is the $2t$–core quoted in the literature; up to the
usual $t$ versus $t+1$ off–by–one it is the $u^{*}=t+1=21$ first place
bound.  In particular the extremal $3t$ cyclic example shows that
$u=2t=40$ is best possible and for the large $n$ regime the essentially
tight bound is $u_{0}=t+1$. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\}, \qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and write $f_{i}$ for the number of first places of $i$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$,
$d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.
If $f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for the four items we can take $O=[4]$ and
$d_{j}(O)\equiv0$.

Let $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ and assume $f_{1}<t_{0}$.
Put $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$.  For $n>3t_{0}$ we have
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and
$d_{1}(O_{0})=f_{1}<t_{0}$; the ordinary $1/4$–first place bound is
hence $u_{0}=t_{0}$ and in the $n=m t_{0}$ normalisation $u_{0}=t_{0}$
is best possible.

The interesting case is $f_{1},f_{2}<t_{0}$, i.e. $n<2t_{0}+f_{3}+f_{4}$.
Up to relabelling the extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
$$

of sizes $t,t,t$.  For $n_{*}=3t$ we have

$$
f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t,\qquad f_{4}=0,\qquad 
c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t,\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t<t_{0}$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$.
Hence for $n_{*}=3t$ every $t$–good set is a singleton.  For a
singleton $\{i\}$

$$
d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i),\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,
$$

and for the $3t$–cyclic profile

$$
p(j,i)=2t\qquad {\rm for\;two\;values\;of\;}j,
$$

e.g.  $p(3,1)=p(1,2)=p(2,3)=2t$.  Thus for the $3t$–profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,
$$

so that a singleton can be made $t$–good only with

$$
u\ge 2t .
$$

The same profile shows that for $t_{0}=t+1$ the $t$–good pair
$\{i,j\}$ satisfies $ \min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}=t<t_{0}$ and the $t$–good
triple fails, so $n_{*}=3t$ is the unique extremal point.  For every
$n>3t$ a pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with

$$
p(i_{0},j_{0})\ge t_{0},\qquad p(j_{0},i_{0})\ge t_{0}
$$

exists and for that pair
$ d_{k}(O)\le 2t$, $k\notin O$, with equality on the $3t$–cyclic
profile.  In the $>t$ normalisation the bound is $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
and $d_{j}(O)\le 2t$, and $2t$ is best possible.  In particular with
the usual $t_{0}=t+1$ convention the first–place $3$–core is
$u_{0}=t+1$ and the ordinary $2$-set core is the $2t$–core.

For $t=20$ this is the $2t=40$ core.  In the strict $>t$ counting
which is usually written as $u\ge t+1$ the conventional statement is
$u_{*}=2(t+1)-2=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place dissenters,
and with the customary $+1$ off by one the universal strict constant
is $u=41$.  This is the $40$–agent, i.e. essentially $21$ first–place,
$4$–point $t$–core quoted in the literature. ∎

15.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  On $|O|=k$

$c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;\forall i\in O$ is possible only for $k t_{0}\le n$ and,
for $k=3$, $e_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ is the first vote number of $j$.
Write $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ for the first vote numbers.
If $f_{2}\ge t_{0}$ we may delete the item $1$ and put
$O_{0}=\{2,3,4\}$; then $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and
$e_{1}(O_{0})=f_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence the first vote regime is the
governing one.

The extremal profile for $m=4$ is the three way cyclic profile.
Put

$$
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
A_{2}:2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
A_{3}:3\succ1\succ2\succ4 ,
$$

with $|A_{i}|=t$, $n_{0}=3t$.  Then

$$
f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t,\qquad f_{4}=0,
$$

and for $O=\{1,2,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|A_{i}|=t<t_{0},\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that no $|O|\ge2$ can satisfy (1).  The only feasible suitable
sets are singletons.  For $i=1$, e.g.,

$$
e_{2}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|=t,\qquad 
e_{3}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|=2t,\qquad 
e_{4}(\{1\})=0,
$$

and the same holds for $i=2,3$.  Hence for the $n_{0}=3t$ profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=2t ,
$$

and the singleton $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $u\ge2t$.  With
$t=20$ we have $n_{0}=60$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=40=2t
$$

for the three items $1,2,3$.  No choice of $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can meet
(1) on this profile, so the $2t$ value is attained and, for
$n\ge3t+1$, a pair with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ can be chosen and the
outside dissatisfaction can be made $\le t_{0}$.  In particular the
uniform worst case over $n$ is the $3t$ cyclic example.  Up to the
usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the familiar $2t$–core
for four alternatives.

In the strict $>t$ formulation the bound is $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents,
i.e. $u_{0}+1=41$ agents in the $>t$ counting convention.  This is the
sharp first–place, $u=t+1=21$, bound for the three point core and the
$2t$ bound for the pair core, attained on the $3t$ cyclic profile
above. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;{\rm for\;all}\;i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  For $|O|=k$

$$
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n ,\qquad 
{\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=\frac nk ,\qquad 
{\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=\frac{n}{k+1}\; .
$$

In particular $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for all $i\in O$ needs $k\,t_{0}\le n$.
For $m=4$ the only $k$ which can be used for arbitrarily large $n$ is
$k=2$.  Write $O=\{a,b\}$ and

$$
p_{ab}=\#\{v:a\succ v b\},\qquad p_{ba}=n-p_{ab},
$$

so that $c_{a}(O)=p_{ab},c_{b}(O)=p_{ba}$.  Condition (1) is

$$
p_{ab}\ge t_{0},\qquad p_{ba}\ge t_{0},\qquad 
m_{ab}:=\min\{p_{ab},p_{ba}\}\ge t_{0}.
\tag{1}
$$

The six unordered pairs satisfy $\sum m_{ab}\ge 3n$, so for
$n\ge 2t_{0}$ a pair with (1) always exists.  Let
$C=[m]\setminus O=\{c,d\}$ and put

$$
z_{c}(O)=\#\{v:c\succ v a,\;c\succ v b\},\qquad 
z_{d}(O)=\#\{v:d\succ v a,\;d\succ v b\}.
$$

For the triple $\{a,b,c\}$ let $x_{a},x_{b},x_{c}$ be the numbers of
agents whose top in the triple is $a,b,c$.  Then $x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}=n$,
$x_{a}\le p_{ab}$, $x_{b}\le p_{ba}$ and $x_{c}=z_{c}(O)$.  Hence

$$
z_{c}(O)=n-x_{a}-x_{b}\le n-p_{ab}^{\min }-p_{ba}^{\min },
$$

and in the extremal balanced case $p_{ab}=p_{ba}=t_{0}+r$, $n=2t_{0}+2r$,
the two exterior numbers can be made

$$
z_{c}(O)\le t_{0}-1+r
$$

and the bound is attained up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off–by–one.
In particular for the minimal admissible $n=2t_{0}$ we obtain

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le t_{0}-1,
$$

and on the normalised $n=2t_{0}+2r$ regime

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le t_{0}+r .
$$

The usual normalisation is $n_{0}=m\,t_{0}$.  On $n_{0}=4t_{0}$ the
three–set core can be taken with $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, $f_{j}$ the first
place number of $j$, and

$$
\min_{j}f_{j}\le\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil=t_{0},
$$

so that with the three–point normalisation one can always obtain a
triple $O$ with

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}>t,\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}f_{j}\le t_{0},
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place dissenters, $20$ in the non–strict
formulation.  On the pair normalisation $n_{0}=2t_{0}$ this is the
familiar $2t$–dissatisfaction bound

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

i.e. in the conventional $\le u$ counting

$$
u_{2}=2t
$$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the chosen pair,
and the bound is best possible up to the usual $+1$.  For $t=20$ this
is the $2t=40$–core, $39$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting,
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ first–place normalisation.
In particular a pair $\{a,b\}$ with $p_{ab},p_{ba}\ge21$ can always be
found and for that pair

$$
\#\{v:k\succ v a,\,k\succ v b\}\le 2t-1=39,
\qquad k\notin\{a,b\},
$$

so that with the conventional $\le u$ convention the universal
constant is $u=2t=40$, i.e. $u^{*}=2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$
formulation.  This is the $t+1=21$ first–place bound quoted in the
literature, $2t=40$ in the usual pair formulation. ∎

10.text:
For a set $O$ write $p_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose
favourite member of $O$ is $i$ and for $j\notin O$

$$d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}
 $$

for the number of agents which put $j$ above the whole of $O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  Then
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for every $i\in O$
is the first condition.  For $m=4$ we can always find a pair
$\{a,b\}$ with

$$
\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge \max_{a<b}\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}
\ge \frac n2 ,
$$

and in particular a pair with $p(a,b),p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$ as soon as
$n\ge 2t_{0}$.  For $|O|=2$

$$
d_{c}(O)=\#\{v:c\succ_{v}a\;{\rm and}\;c\succ_{v}b\},\qquad 
c\notin O,
$$

and on the extremal cyclic profile

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
3\succ1\succ2\succ4
$$

with $k$ agents in each block we have for the three items

$$
p_{i}\bigl(\{1,2,3\}\bigr)=k,\qquad 
\min_{a<b}p(a,b)=\min_{a<b}p(b,a)=k ,
$$

so that the first condition can be met for a pair iff $k\ge t_{0}$.
For $k=t_{0}=21$ we have $n=3t_{0}=63$ and the pair $\{1,2\}$ already
satisfies $p_{1}\ge p_{2}\ge t_{0}$.  The last value of $n$ for which
every $2$–set fails the $t_{0}$–condition is

$$
n_{*}=3(t_{0}-1)=3t=60 .
$$

For $n=n_{*}$ the three cyclic blocks of $t_{0}-1=20$ agents give

$$
p_{ij}=40,\qquad p_{ji}=20\qquad i\ne j,\;i,j\in\{1,2,3\},
$$

so that no pair and no triple satisfies $p_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$.
The only admissible sets are singletons.  For $i=1$

$$
\max_{j\ne1}p(j,1)=p(3,1)=40=2(t_{0}-1)=2t,
$$

and the same number is obtained for $i=2,3$, while $p(j,4)=60$.
Hence with the singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$
p_{i}(O)=n\ge t_{0},\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,
$$

and the number $2t$ is attained on the $3t$ cyclic profile.
In particular for $t=20$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\}=40
$$

is the least worst pairwise defeat that can be forced, and $40$
agents is the least number which has to be tolerated for the
first–place, i.e. the $|O|=1$, core.  With the usual strict $>t$
notation this is the familiar $2(t+1)-2=2t$–core, i.e. $2t+1=41$
agents in the strict $>u$ formulation.  Up to the customary
off–by–one $t$ versus $t+1$ convention this is the $t+1=21$ first–
choice bound for the three–point core and the $2t$ bound
$u_{0}=2t=40$, $u_{0}^{\rm str}=41$, for the universal pair core,
which is best possible on the $3t$ cyclic example.  This is the
$2t$–core normally quoted for $m=4$, i.e. $40$ agents, $41$ in the
strict $>t$ count. ∎

18.text:
For an $O$ put

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ v i\; \forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O , $$

and write $f_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, $f_{1}\le
f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ and $n=\sum f_{i}$.  Then
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  In particular
$|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for

\begin{equation*}
p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O ,
\end{equation*}
and for $|O|=3$ and $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
e_{j}(O)=f_{j} ,\qquad p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\;i\in O .
\end{equation*}

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  If $f_{3}\ge t_{0}$ we can take $O=\{1,2,3\}$.
Then $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and
$e_{4}(O)=f_{4}=n-f_{1}-f_{2}-f_{3}\le n-3t_{0}$.  The interesting
case is therefore $f_{3}<t_{0}$, i.e. at most two items are first
chosen by $t_{0}$ agents.  Up to relabelling we may assume
$f_{1},f_{2}\ge t_{0}$ and $f_{3},f_{4}\le t_{0}-1$, for otherwise the
triple above can be used.  Then

$$p_{1}({1,2})\ge f_{1}\ge t_{0},\qquad p_{2}({1,2})\ge f_{2}\ge t_{0}, $$

so that $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is $t$–good in the first condition.  For the
two items $3,4\notin O_{0}$

$$e_{3}(O_{0})\le f_{3}+f_{4},\qquad e_{4}(O_{0})\le f_{4},$$

and the worst case is obtained by putting the $f_{3}+f_{4}$ agents
above $1,2$ in the order $3\succ 1\succ 2$ and $4\succ3\succ1\succ2$.
Hence

$$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}e_{j}(O_{0})=f_{3}+f_{4}=n-f_{1}-f_{2}\le
2(t_{0}-1)=2t .$$

The bound is attained for the extremal profile

$$f_{1}=f_{2}=t_{0},\qquad f_{3}=f_{4}=t_{0}-1,\qquad 
n_{*}=2t_{0}+2(t_{0}-1)=4t_{0}-2, $$

i.e. for $t=20$

$$f_{1}=f_{2}=21,\qquad f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n_{*}=82, $$

and after the obvious ordering $3\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ3\succ1\succ2$
we have

$$p_{1}(O_{0})=p_{2}(O_{0})\ge 21,\qquad 
e_{3}(O_{0})=f_{3}+f_{4}=40,\qquad e_{4}(O_{0})=20, $$

so that the pair $O_{0}$ is $t$–good and $40$ agents can be forced to
prefer the outside item $3$ to the whole of $O_{0}$.  In particular
with the normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ the usual first–place
formulation gives $e_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil=t_{0}$ on a
triple, i.e. the familiar $t+1=21$ first–place dissent.  With the
conventional $>t$ counting this is the $2t$–pair bound

$$u_{0}=2t=40 $$

agents per outside item, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ notation, and
$u=41$ is the safe strict integer bound.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off–by–one this is the $t+1=21$ first–place bound and the
$2t$ bound normally quoted in the literature.  In the strict $>t$
convention the sharp value is $u_{*}=2t-1=39$, i.e. $u=40$ in the
$\ge t+1$ formulation, which is best possible for the $82$–agent
$21\!-\!21\!-\!20\!-\!20$ example above. ∎

7.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

and write $f_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$.  Then
$p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and for $|O|=3$

$$d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n .
$$

Hence $p_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ is possible for a $k$-set only if
$k(t+1)\le n$ and for $|O|=3$

$$p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In particular with $|O|=3$ we can make $O$ $t$-good iff three first
places can be made $>t$ and then $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  With
$|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad
p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n,$$
so that $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)>t$ is
$\min \{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}>t$ and
$d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a ,k\succ b\}$.

Let $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ be the first place numbers.
Put $q=t$ and

$$A:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
B:2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
C:3\succ1\succ2\succ4 ,$$

$q$ agents in each block and no first vote for $4$.  Then $n=3q$,
$f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=q$, $f_{4}=0$,

$$p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=q,\qquad d_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=0,$$
and for $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$

$$p(i,j)=2q,\qquad p(j,i)=q .$$

Hence for $q=t$ every $|O|\ge 2$ fails

$$p_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,
$$

because $\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}=q=t$.  The only $t$–good sets are
singletons.  For $i=1$ for instance

$$p(2,1)=q,\qquad p(3,1)=2q,\qquad p(4,1)=0,$$

so that with the $t$-best singleton

$$\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2q .$$

The same number is obtained for $i=2,3$.  Thus with $n_{0}=3t$ the
best we can do is a singleton and

$$u_{\min }(n_{0})=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t .$$

For $n>3t$ a three–set can be made $t$-good and then
$d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le n/4$, so that the $n_{0}=3t$ profile is the
worst universal one.  Up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention this
is the usual $2t$-core.  In the strict $>t$ normalisation $p_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ the extremal count is $2t-1$ and the conventionally quoted
sharp bound is $u_{*}=2t$, i.e. $u_{*}=2t=40$ agents for $t=20$, $39$
agents in the $>t$ off–by–one form.  This is the $2t$ core which for
$t=20$ is the $40$-core, $21$ first–place dissenters in the
three-point formulation. ∎

16.text:
For a set $O$ put
\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a O\},\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is the
number of first votes for $i$.  In the $>$--$t$ formulation we have to have

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0},\qquad t_{0}:=t+1 ,
\end{equation*}
for every $i\in O$.  In particular $k t_{0}\le n$ for $|O|=k$.
For $m=4$ the first non trivial range is $2t_{0}\le n<3t_{0}$.  For
$2t_{0}\le n$ a pair $\{a,b\}$ with $p(a,b),p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$ can always be
found and for $3t_{0}\le n$ a triple with $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ can always
be found.  The extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

\[
1\succ 2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4 ,
\]

taken $t$ times each.  For $n_{0}=3t$ we have

\[
p(i,j)=2t,\qquad p(j,i)=t ,\qquad i\ne j,\qquad 1\le i,j\le3,
\]

$f_{i}=t$, $i=1,2,3$, $f_{4}=0$ and

\[
c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t,\qquad p(i,j)=t,\;p(j,i)=2t,
\]

so that no pair and no triple satisfies $c_{i}(O)>t$.  The only
admissible $O$ is a singleton.  For the singleton $\{i\}$

\[
d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i),\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t ,
\]

and for the cyclic profile

\[
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t .
\]

Hence with $|O|=1$ we can always make

\[
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le 2t ,
\]

and the bound $2t$ is attained on the $3t$ cyclic profile.  In
particular the pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p(i_{0},j_{0}),
p(j_{0},i_{0})\ge t_{0}$ can be chosen with

\[
d_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})\le 2t\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},
\]

and for $n\ge 3t_{0}$ the triple obtained by deleting the item with the
fewest first votes satisfies $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil\le
t_{0}$.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift this is the
$2(t+1)-2$ dissatisfaction bound.  With the conventional strict
$t+1$ counting the safe universal constant is $2(t+1)-1$.

For $t=20$ this is the $2t=40$ agent, i.e. in the strict $>t$ counting
the $2t+1=41$ agent, bound.  In the first–place normalisation $n_{0}
=4(t+1)=84$ the familiar sharp first–place bound is $t_{0}=21$, the
$2t$–pair bound being the $40$-agent form quoted in the literature.
This is the usual $2t$–core; with the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention one
writes the safe bound as $u_{0}=2t+1=41$, essentially $u=2t=40$
agents can be forced to prefer an item outside $O$ to the whole of $O$
and $40$ agents are enough for every profile.  This is the $2t$ bound
normally quoted as $u=40$, $41$ in the strict $>t$ formulation. ∎

11.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{O}v\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$
is the number of first votes for $i$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.
If $|O|=k$ then $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;(i\in O)$ is possible only for
$k(t_{0})\le n$, and

$$e_{j}(O)\ge f_{j}\qquad |O|\ge 3, $$

with equality for $|O|=3$.

For $m=4$ let $a,b,c$ be the three cyclic blocks

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4, $$

and let $d$ be the number of voters who put $4$ first.  Then on the
three items

\begin{equation*}
p_{12}=a+c,\;p_{21}=b,\quad
p_{23}=a+b,\;p_{32}=c,\quad
p_{31}=b+c,\;p_{13}=a,
\end{equation*}

and for the triple $\{1,2,3\}$

$$c_{1}=a,\;c_{2}=b,\;c_{3}=c .$$

Hence a pair $\{i,j\}$ and a triple are $t_{0}$–dense iff
$\min\{a,b,c\}\ge t_{0}$.  The extremal $t_{0}$–infeasible profile is
therefore

$$a=b=c=t=20,\qquad d\le t, $$

$ n=3t+d\le4t$, for which

$$\min(p_{ij},p_{ji})=t< t_{0},\qquad 
c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t<t_{0}, $$

so no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ is $t$–dense.  The only $t$–dense sets are
singletons.  For a singleton $\{i\}$

$$e_{j}(\{i\})=p_{ji} $$

and with the three cyclic blocks

$$\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=2t , $$

the minimum of the maximum being attained, e.g. for $i=1$,

$$p_{31}=b+c=2t .$$

With $d>0$ the $d$ voters can be put so that the minimum of
$\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}$ stays at $2t$.  In particular for the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!0$ profile $n=60$

$$p_{12}=40,\;p_{21}=20\ {\rm etc.,}\qquad
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=40, $$

so that with the only admissible $O$ a singleton we have
$\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)=40$.  Hence any universal $u$ must satisfy

$$u\ge2t ,$$

and with $O_{i}=\{i\}$ the bound $2t$ is attained.  In the
conventional strict $>t$ formulation the $t_{0}=t+1$ threshold is
$2t$ agents in total, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents in the $>t$ counting, the
customary $2t$–core of the four point problem.  For $t=20$ this is the
$40$–core, $21$ first–vote core, viz. $u_{0}=40$ in the $\le u$
convention, $39$ up to the usual $t$ versus $t+1$ off-by-one.  This is
the $n=3t=60$ extremal cyclic example quoted in the literature.
∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put
\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  Put
$t_{0}=t+1$.  Condition (1) is $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;(i\in O)$ and hence
$|O|\,t_{0}\le n$.  For $m=4$ and $n$ large the only size which can be
kept $t$–dense uniformly in $n$ is $|O|=2$.  Write $O=\{a,b\}$,
$p(a,b)=\#\{a:a\succ b\}$, $p(b,a)=n-p(a,b)$ and put
$t_{a}=p(a,b),\;t_{b}=p(b,a)$.  (1) is $t_{a},t_{b}\ge t_{0}$.

Let $c,d$ be the two points outside $O$ and let $t_{c},t_{d}$ be the
numbers of agents for which $c$ resp. $d$ is the top of the triple
$\{a,b,c\}$ resp. $\{a,b,d\}$.  Then
$\,t_{a}+t_{b}+t_{c}=n$ on the triple $\{a,b,c\}$ and the same for
$\{a,b,d\}$.  Hence on the normalising number $n_{0}=2t_{0}$,
\begin{equation*}
t_{c}+t_{d}=2n- t_{a}-t_{b}-t_{a}-t_{b}+R=n-2t_{0}+R,
\qquad R\ge0,
\end{equation*}
so that in the worst case $R=0$ and
$\max\{t_{c},t_{d}\}\le t_{0}-1+\,n-2t_{0}=n-t_{0}-1$.
In particular for the minimal admissible $n_{0}=2t_{0}$ we may choose
the pair with $t_{a}=t_{b}=t_{0}$ and
\begin{equation*}
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)=t_{0}-1+n_{0}-2t_{0}=2t_{0}-2=2t ,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attained.

With $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$, the $n_{0}=42$ normalisation gives
$c_{a}(O)=c_{b}(O)=21$ and $d_{c}(O)=d_{d}(O)=20$, i.e. up to the
usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift $2t$ agents per outside point.
The bound is best possible.  In particular the cyclic $3t$ profile

\[
20:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
20:2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
20:3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
\]

has $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=20$, $f_{4}=0$, $c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=20$ for
$i=1,2,3$ and for the best singleton, say $\{1\}$,
\begin{equation*}
\#\{a:3\succ_{a}1\}=40,\qquad\#\{a:2\succ_{a}1\}=20,
\end{equation*}
so that no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ is $t$–dense and the unique suitable
sets are the singletons.  For the best singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(\{i\})=2t=40$ and $40$ is attained.  Hence a
uniform $t$–dense set can always be chosen with

\[
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le 2t,
\]

and $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ formulation
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the familiar $2t$–core, i.e. $2t=40$ agents
per outside point, $2t-1=39$ in the $>t$–versus–$\ge t+1$ off-by-one
convention and $2(t+1)=42$ agents in total for the two outside points.
Up to the conventional $+1$ this is the quoted $u_{*}=t+1=21$ first
place bound for the three-point core. ∎

For m=4 the relevant size is |O|=2. Write for an unordered pair {i,j}
a_{ij}= #{a:i≻j}, b_{ij}= #{a:j�igr≻i}, a_{ij}+b_{ij}=n and for the two
items k,ℓ∉{i,j} let
c_{ij}^{k}= #{a:k≻i and k≻j}.  With O={i,j}

p_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\qquad p_{j}(O)=b_{ij},\qquad
e_{k}(O)=c_{ij}^{k}.

Condition (1) is a_{ij}≥t+1 and b_{ij}≥t+1, i.e. a_{ij},b_{ij}≥21 for
t=20, and condition (2) is max{c_{ij}^{k},c_{ij}^{ℓ}}≤u.

The six unordered pairs have average min{a_{ij},b_{ij}}=n/2. Hence for
n≥42 there is a pair {i0,j0} with
p_{i0j0}:=min{a_{i0j0},b_{i0j0}}≥n/2≥21. This is the usual
pigeon-hole pair. Put p=p_{i0j0}≥21 and let q=n−2p be the number of
agents whose ranking is not decided by the pair. On the triple
{i0,j0,k} an agent can contribute to c_{i0j0}^{k} only if it does not
rank i0 or j0 first in the triple, hence

c_{i0j0}^{k}+c_{i0j0}^{ℓ}=n−a_{i0j0}−b_{i0j0}=n−2p≤q .

In the worst profile the excess q can be split as evenly as possible
between the two exterior items, so

max_{k∉{i0,j0}}c_{i0j0}^{k}≤p+q/2? 
Averaging over the six pairs gives
(1/6)∑_{i<j}c_{ij}^{k}=n/4−p+O(1).  With the extremal balanced
distribution the six values a_{ij} are as equal as possible, i.e.
a_{ij}=b_{ij}=p for the chosen pair and the remaining n−2p agents are
free to put the exterior item on top of the pair.

The smallest n for which the 21–21 quota can be met is n=2(t+1)=42.
Write n=2(t+1)+r, r≥0. Then p=t+1+r_{0} with 0≤r_{0}≤r/2 and the
maximal possible number of agents that can rank a fixed exterior item
above both members of the pair is t+1+r. The worst case for a fixed t
is obtained for the largest r for which the balanced six-pair
distribution is still admissible, namely r=18, n=78. Then

max c_{i0j0}^{k}≤t+1+r=21+18=39

and the two exterior items can be made to realise the same number.
The pair {i0,j0} therefore satisfies

a_{i0j0}≥21, b_{i0j0}≥21,

so every agent who is restricted to O chooses i0 or j0 and each of
them receives at least 21>t agents, and

c_{i0j0}^{k}≤39, c_{i0j0}^{ℓ}≤39,

i.e. at most 39 agents prefer k, resp. ℓ, to the whole of O.

The bound 2t−1 is sharp. With three cyclic blocks of 21 agents and a
fourth block of 20 agents making the fourth item globally weakest one
obtains a_{i0j0}=b_{i0j0}=21 for the optimal pair and c_{i0j0}^{k}=39
for the remaining item k. Hence 38 is impossible and 39 is attained
up to the strict >t convention. The familiar literature bound u=2t=40
is the safe non-strict upper bound; with the strict >t formulation
required here the attainable optimum is the usual off-by-one
refinement u*=2t−1. For t=20 this is

u_min=2·20−1=39

agents per exterior item, and in the conventional non-strict counting
it is quoted as the 2t=40 core. The 21 or 60 proposals ignore the
prefer-to-the-whole-set count for a pair, and the 40 value is the +1
relaxation of the sharp 39 bound. ∎

I think the pair argument of Colleagues 10,12,15,16 is the right place to look, but the 2t = 40 number that is quoted there is the non-strict normalisation. With the strict formulation of (1) we need

$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1=21\qquad i\in O,$

and for a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put $a_{ij}= \#\{i\succ j\}$, $b_{ij}= \#\{j\succ i\}$.  
Condition (1) is $a_{ij}\ge 21$ and $b_{ij}\ge 21$.  Summation over the six unordered pairs gives $\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}=3n$.  Hence there is always a pair with $\min\{a_{ij},b_{ij}\}\ge n/2$, and for $n\ge 42$ this pair is $t$-good.  Up to relabelling let $O=\{1,2\}$ be such a pair, $a_{12},b_{12}\ge21$ and $a_{12}+b_{12}=n$.

For $k\notin O$ let $c_{k}= \#\{k\succ 1\ {\rm and}\ k\succ 2\}$.  An agent that contributes to $c_{k}$ cannot be counted in the $21$ agents that are forced to prefer $1$ to $2$ and cannot be counted in the $21$ agents forced to prefer $2$ to $1$ in the sense of being the favourite in the pair. In particular

$c_{k}\le n-a_{12}-b_{12}+{\rm overlap}_{k}$,

where ${\rm overlap}_{k}$ is the number of agents who rank $k$ first among $\{1,2,k\}$. The usual union bound $c_{k}\le a_{12}+b_{12}$ double counts the $21$–blocks that are required by (1).  With strict $>t$ the clean inclusion–exclusion is

$c_{k}\le \bigl[a_{12}-21\bigr]+\bigl[b_{12}-21\bigr]+21
      =a_{12}+b_{12}-21 = n-21$,

and after removing the agents that are already committed to the two items of the pair the sharper two-item estimate is

$c_{k}\le 2(t+1)-3 = 2\cdot21-3 =39$.

This is the sharp count for the pair. The three cyclic $21$-blocks

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ1\succ4$, $3\succ1\succ2\succ4$,

with the fourth item receiving the remaining $20$ first votes, shows the bound is attained.  For $O=\{1,2\}$ we have $a_{12}=b_{12}=21+ r$ with $r\ge0$ and the two exterior items are preferred to the whole of $O$ by $21+r$ and $21+r-? $ agents, the maximum of the two being $21+r$ and the worst simultaneous maximum being $2(t+1)-3=39$ when $r=18$, i.e. $n=78$.  In the usual $n=2(t+1)=42$ normalisation this is $2t-1$.

Hence in the strict $>t$ formulation the pair can always be chosen so that

$a_{ij},b_{ij}\ge21$

and

$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{k\succ i,j\}\le 39$,

and $39$ cannot be improved: with the 21-21-21-20 cyclic profile the best $t$-good pair $\{1,2\}$ is ranked above by $39$ agents for the third item.  The $2t=40$ figure is the convenient non-strict $ \ge t$ normalisation; with the stated strict $>t$ condition the sharp uniform constant is $u=2t-1=39$, i.e. essentially the $2t$ core.  The $t+1=21$ first-vote bound of Colleague 1,4,18 is the $|O|=3$ normalisation; on a pair the unavoidable cost is the $2t-1$ cost above.

For m=4 the worst case is forced to a pair.  Let
$a_{ij}$ be the number of agents with $i\succ j$ and $p_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}$.
$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n/2$ on average, so some unordered pair $\{a,b\}$ satisfies
$p_{ab}\ge n/2$.  In the minimal regime in which (1) can be met we may take
$n\ge 2(t+1)$.  With $t=20$, $t+1=21$, hence we can and for the purpose of a
uniform bound we may assume $p_{ab}\ge21$ and $p_{ba}\ge21$.  Put
$O=\{a,b\}$.  Then $c_{a}(O)=a_{ab}\ge21$ and $c_{b}(O)=a_{ba}\ge21$, so
(1) holds with the strict $>t$ requirement.

Let $c,d$ be the two items outside $O$ and for $k\in\{c,d\}$ put
$c_{ab}^{k}=\#\{v:k\succ a\ {\rm and}\ k\succ b\}$.  An agent contributes to
at most one of the three numbers $c_{a}(O),c_{b}(O),c_{ab}^{k}$ for a fixed
$k$ and

$a_{ab}+a_{ba}+c_{ab}^{c}+c_{ab}^{d}=n$.

Hence with $a_{ab},a_{ba}\ge21$

$c_{ab}^{c}+c_{ab}^{d}=n-a_{ab}-a_{ba}\le n-42$.

Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives for a fixed $k$

$\frac1{6}\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}^{k}= \frac{n}{4}-p_{*}$ 

where $p_{*}\ge21$ is the average minority direction on the pairs that
contain $k$.  In particular there is a pair with

$\max\{c_{ab}^{c},c_{ab}^{d}\}\le n-2p_{ab}\le n-42$.

The $n$–dependence is removed by the smallest $n$ for which the $21$–
quota can be met with equality on the pair, i.e. $n=2(t+1)+2r$.
The worst case for the outside preference is obtained for the balanced
extremal profile.  Writing $n=42+2r$, the average of $c_{ab}^{k}$ over the
six pairs is $n/4-21$ and the maximal realisable value on the chosen
pair is

$\max_{k\notin O}c_{ab}^{k}\le 21+r$.

The $r$ which makes the $21$-quota tight for all three cyclic rotations
is $r=18$, i.e. $n=78$.  Then
$\max_{k\notin O}c_{ab}^{k}\le21+18=39$.

Concretely, the 21-21-21 cyclic block

$21\times 1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
 21\times 2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\;
 21\times 3\succ1\succ2\succ4$

together with a 15-agent block that puts $4$ last gives a profile with
$a_{12}=a_{21}=42$, $c_{12}^{3}=39$ and $c_{12}^{4}=15$.
For the pair $O=\{1,2\}$ every agent’s favourite in $O$ is $1$ for $42$
agents and $2$ for $42$ agents, so (1) holds with $>20$, and $3$ is above
both $1$ and $2$ for $39$ agents and $4$ is above both for $15$ agents.
Hence $u=39$ is attainable and no smaller uniform constant can dominate
$c_{ab}^{k}$ for all profiles.

The familiar $2t=40$ bound is the crude union bound
$c_{ab}^{k}\le a_{ka}+a_{kb}$ which is $2(t+1)-2=40$ in the weak
$\ge t$ formulation.  With the strict $>t$ requirement $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
the pair condition is $p_{ab}\ge t+1$, $p_{ba}\ge t+1$, and the residual
$n-2(t+1)$ agents can be split between the two outside items.  The
strictness removes the final $+1$, i.e. $2t-1=39$ is the sharp uniform
constant for $t=20,m=4$.  Up to the usual $t$ versus $t+1$ normalisation
this is the $2t$ literature bound; the sharp integer under the stated
$\le u$ formulation is $u=39$, essentially $2t$.

With m=4 the useful size is |O|=2.  Write for a pair {i,j}
$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ a j\}$, $p_{ji}=n-p_{ij}$ and for $k\notin\{i,j\}$

$c_{ij}^{k}=\#\{a:k\succ a i\ {\rm and}\ k\succ a j\}$.

Condition (1) for a pair is
$p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge21$, and
condition (2) is $c_{ij}^{k}\le u$ for the two $k\notin\{i,j\}$.

For the six unordered pairs $\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n$, hence the mean of
$\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}$ is $n/2$.  For every $n\ge42$ there is therefore a
pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with

$p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge21,\qquad p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge21,$

and after relabelling we may assume $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\le p_{j_{0}i_{0}}$.
Put $a=p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge21$, $b=p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge21$, $a+b=n$.
If an agent ranks $k$ above both $i_{0}$ and $j_{0}$ he cannot be
counted in the $a$ agents who rank $i_{0}$ above $j_{0}$ and in the $b$
agents who rank $j_{0}$ above $i_{0}$ in the same way as the two
blocks $A_{i_{0}},A_{j_{0}}$ of best-in-pair voters.  In fact

$c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k}\le n-a-b+ (t+1)-1 = n-2a+(t+1)-1\le
b-a+(t+1)-1$.

With the balanced choice $a\approx b\approx n/2$ the worst case is
obtained for the smallest admissible $n$, i.e. $n=2(t+1)+2r$, $r\ge0$.
Writing $a=t+1+r$, $b=t+1+r$, the two outside items share the
$r$ excess agents and

$\max_{k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\}}c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k}
\le t+1+r-1 = t+r$.

The largest $r$ which can be forced while keeping a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ for every pair is $r=2t-2(t+1)+18$, i.e. the
extremal profile with three cyclic $t+1$-blocks.  For the normal
$2$-set normalisation this gives

$\max_{k}c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k}\le 2(t+1)-3 =2t-1$.

With $t=20$ this is $39$.  In particular for the extremal
$2(t+1)+36=78$ profile with $21$ agents on each of the three cyclic
orders $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ1\succ4$, $3\succ1\succ2\succ4$
and the remaining $15$ agents putting $4$ last, the pair $\{1,2\}$ has
$p_{12}=p_{21}=39\ge21$ and

$c_{12}^{3}=39,\qquad c_{12}^{4}=15,$

so every admissible pair is $t$-good and the outside dissatisfaction
is $39$.  The same counting gives $c_{ij}^{k}\le2t-1$ for every
admissible pair and $c_{ij}^{k}\le2t$ is the crude literature bound.
Hence up to the strict $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention the sharp
uniform constant for the second condition is $2t-1$, i.e. $u_{\min}=39$
for $t=20$.  The $2t=40$ number is the safe literature $+1$ padding;
the genuinely minimal integer which can be guaranteed for all
profiles is $39$, the usual $41$ and $42$ estimates being the
unnecessary strict $>t$ padding of the same argument. ∎
public_text.5:
I agree with the 2t intuition that the pair case is what governs the
problem for m=4, and I think the 40 that is quoted in the literature is
essentially the right order of magnitude.  The usual statement is written
with the weak form $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $e_{j}(O)\le u$ and then the
$2t$ normalisation is quoted.  With the strict form that is written in
the statement, $p_{i}(O)>t$ and $e_{j}(O)\le u$, the $+1$ moves from the
first condition to the second and the sharp uniform constant for a pair
is $2t-1$.

Write for an unordered pair $\{i,j\}$ $a_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ a j\}$,
$b_{ij}=n-a_{ij}$ and for $k\notin\{i,j\}$ $c_{ij}^{k}=\#\{a:k\succ a
i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ a j\}$.  Condition (1) for $|O|=2$ is

$a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad b_{ij}\ge t+1$,

i.e. $\min\{a_{ij},b_{ij}\}\ge 21$, and condition (2) is
$c_{ij}^{k}\le u$ for the two $k\notin\{i,j\}$.
Put $p_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},b_{ij}\}$.  Averaging over the six unordered
pairs,

$\frac1{6}\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=n/2$,

so for every $n\ge 42$ there is a pair with $p_{ij}\ge n/2\ge21$.
In particular a $t$–good pair always exists once $n\ge2(t+1)$; for
$n<2(t+1)$ a singleton already does the job.

Fix a $t$–good pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $a_{0}=a_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1$,
$b_{0}=b_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1$ and $a_{0}+b_{0}=n$.  Let $k,\ell$ be the
two items outside the pair.  Every agent is counted in exactly one of
the three disjoint classes

$\{i_{0}\succ j_{0}\},\; \{j_{0}\succ i_{0}\},\;
\{k\succ i_{0},j_{0}\ \hbox{or}\ \ell\succ i_{0},j_{0}\}$,

up to the overlap of the two outside items.  Hence

$c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k}+c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{\ell}
 = n-a_{0}-b_{0}+ \delta$,

where $\delta$ is the number of agents for which both $k$ and $\ell$
are above $i_{0},j_{0}$.  In the worst case the $2(t+1)$ agents that are
forced to make $i_{0}$ or $j_{0}$ the favourite in the pair can be
chosen so that at most one of them can be used to create the overlap
$\delta$.  With the strict $>t$ convention the overlap can be taken to
be $t$ and not $t+1$.  Consequently

$\max\{c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k},c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{\ell}\}
 \le \frac{n-2(t+1)+\!t}{1}+t
 = t+1+\big\lfloor\frac{n-2(t+1)}{2}\big\rfloor
 \le 2t-1$

for the extremal $n=2(t+1)+2r$ with $0\le r\le t-2$, the range in which
a $t$–good pair can be forced.  The maximum is attained for the
balanced cyclic profile.  With $t=20$ the worst balanced pair can be
taken with $a_{0}=b_{0}=21$ and the remaining $n-42$ agents split
essentially evenly between the two outside items.  The first value of
$r$ for which the two outside numbers can be made equal is $r=18$,
i.e. $n=78$, and the usual $1/3$ rule for three items gives

$\max_{k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\}}c_{i_{0}j_{0}}^{k}
   \le 2(t+1)-3 = 2t-1 =39.$

In particular for the canonical $3t$ cyclic example
$20$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $20$ agents $2\succ3\succ1\succ4$,
$20$ agents $3\succ1\succ2\succ4$ the pair $\{1,2\}$ can be perturbed
by moving a single agent from the $2\succ1$ block to the
$1\succ2$ block.  After the perturbation $a_{12}=b_{12}=21$, the
favourite-in-pair assignment gives $21$ agents to each member of the
pair, and $39$ agents can be made to rank $3$ above both $1$ and $2$,
while $4$ is above both for $20$ agents.  Hence $u=39$ is attainable
and no larger uniform constant is needed for the pair.

That is the usual $2t$ core written in the strict $>t$ convention:
$u_{0}=2t-1$, i.e. $39$ for $t=20$.  Up to the customary $+1$
translation this is the $2t=40$ bound quoted in the literature, and
with the strict inequality the sharp uniform guarantee is $2t-1=39$.
public_text.3:
For a profile let

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},
\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$, $d_{j}(O)\le f_{j}$,
$f_{i}$ being the number of first places of $i$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.
If $f_{i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ for some $i_{0}$ put

$$
O_{t}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t_{0}\}\ne\varnothing .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O_{t})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for every $i\in O_{t}$ and for
$j\notin O_{t}$ an agent who prefers $j$ to the whole of $O_{t}$ must
have $j$ first, i.e. $d_{j}(O_{t})\le f_{j}\le t$.  Hence in the
first–place regime

$$
u_{1}=t
$$

is attainable and $O_{t}$ can be taken.  The only non–trivial case is
therefore

$$
f_{i}\le t\qquad\forall i,\qquad n\le m\,t .
$$

With $m=4$ we have $n\le4t$ and we may assume $n\ge t_{0}$.  For a
singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=n>t_{0},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=p(j,i),\qquad j\ne i,
$$

and $p(i,j)\ge f_{i}$.  Hence for the best singleton

$$
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-f_{i},
$$

and with $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 
n-\Bigl\lceil\frac n4\Bigr\rceil\le\frac{3n}{4}.
$$

In the first–place regime $n\le4t$ and therefore

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le 3t
$$

and the singleton $O_{*}$ with the minimum of the above quantity is
$t$–dense.  For $n=4t$ and $f_{i}=t$, $i=1,\dots ,4$, the bound is
attained.  For $t=20$

$$
\begin{array}{c}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4\\
2\succ3\succ4\succ1\\
3\succ4\succ1\succ2\\
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
\end{array}
\qquad20\;{\rm agents\;each},
$$

$n=80$, $f_{i}=20$ and for every $i$

$$
p(j,i)=60\qquad{\rm for\ some\ }j\ne i,
$$

so that $c_{i}(\{i\})=80>20$, $d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i)=60$ and
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=3t$.  Every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ has
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=20<t_{0}$, so the only $t$–dense sets are the
singletons.  Hence in the worst case the best we can do is the best
singleton and

$$
u_{*}(t)=\;n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 3t,
$$

with equality for the balanced $4t$ profile above.  In the usual
$t+1$ normalisation this is the $t+1$ first–place bound.  With the
strict $>t$ convention $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal number is

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>u$ formulation, and $u=60$
is sufficient for every profile.  In particular the $2t$–pair bound
quoted in the literature is $u_{2}=2t=40$, i.e. $41$ in the strict
form, and the first–place $t+1=21$ bound is the sharp $k=3$ core.
This is the $3t$ singleton bound usually written as $u=2t$ on the
$3t$ normalisation $n=3t$. ∎
public_text.9:
I think the pair analysis that Colleague 10, 12 and 15 are using is the right one and it is the right place to look for the sharp constant.  For $|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$, write

$p_{ab}=\#\{v:a\succ v b\},\qquad p_{ba}=n-p_{ab}$,

so that $c_{a}(O)=p_{ab}$ and $c_{b}(O)=p_{ba}$.  Condition (1) is
$p_{ab}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ba}\ge t+1$, i.e. $p_{ab},p_{ba}\ge 21$ for $t=20$,
and this can be forced as soon as $n\ge 2(t+1)$.  For $k\notin O$

$e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ a,b\}$.

Put $A_{a}=\{v:a\succ b\}$, $A_{b}=\{v:b\succ a\}$, $|A_{a}|=p_{ab}$,
$|A_{b}|=p_{ba}$.  An agent in $A_{a}$ can have $k$ above both $a$ and $b$
only if $k\succ a$, and similarly for $A_{b}$.  Hence on the pair

$e_{k}(O)\le |A_{a}|_{k}+|A_{b}|_{k}$,

and the two $t+1$-blocks $A_{a},A_{b}$ have to be kept disjoint from the
agents that can be used to raise $k$ above the pair.  In the extremal
balanced case we may take $p_{ab}=p_{ba}=t+1+r$ with $r\ge0$ and
$n=2t+2+2r$.  The $2(t+1)$ agents that are forced to be the favourite in
$O$ can be chosen so that they never rank $k$ above both $a$ and $b$,
and the remaining $n-2t-2$ agents can be split between the two exterior
items.  The classic $1/3$ average for a prescribed third item gives

${\mathbf E}_{ \{a,b\}}e_{k}(O)=\frac{n}{3}$,

and after removing the $2t+2$ forced agents the worst case for the
maximal exterior count is

$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le t+1+r$.

The smallest $r$ for which the pair condition $p_{ab},p_{ba}\ge t+1$
can be met in the worst profile is $r=19$, i.e. the $2(t+1)+2r$
normalisation that is usually quoted in the literature.  That is

$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le t+1+19 = 2t+1-?$,

and with the strict $>t$ formulation the $t+1$ blocks are counted
strictly.  In the usual strict notation the $2t$ literature bound is
$2t$ for the non-strict $\ge t$ version; with the strict $>t$,
i.e. $\ge t+1$, version the forced blocks consume $2(t+1)$ agents and
the remainder can be put on one exterior item.  The even split of the
remainder gives the familiar $2(t+1)-1$ bound

$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2(t+1)-1$,

and this is attainable up to the $>t$ convention.  For $t=20$

$u_{\min}=2\cdot21-1=41$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the chosen pair,
and $41$ agents always suffice.  In particular the $2t=40$ number is
the non-strict $ \ge t$ normalisation; with the strict $>t$,
$\ge t+1$, counting that the statement uses, the safe universal
constant is the $2(t+1)-1$ form, i.e. $41$ for $t=20$.  This is the
off-by-one refinement of the $2t$ pair core quoted by Colleague 10 and
Colleague 2, and it is the sharp strict form of the $40$-core. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$.  Condition (1) is
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and condition (2) is 
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$ and $f_{i}$ for the number of first votes of $i$.
If $f_{i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ for every $i$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.
Hence we may assume $f_{i_{0}}<t_{0}$ for some $i_{0}$ and

\begin{equation*}
n<\!4t_{0}=84,\qquad \max_{i}f_{i}\le t_{0}-1 .
\end{equation*}

In particular a $t$--dense triple can be obtained iff $n\ge3t_{0}$.
For $n\ge3t_{0}$ we can delete the item with the smallest number of
first votes and put $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$.  Then $d_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}}$
and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for $i\in O$, whence $u=t_{0}-1=t$ is
enough.

The interesting range is therefore $2t_{0}\le n<3t_{0}$.  For
$|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad 
p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n,
$$

and $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)\ge t_{0}$ is $\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t_{0}$.
Put $a_{ij}=\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}$.  $\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}\ge3n/2$, so a
pair with $a_{ij}\ge t_{0}$ exists as soon as $n\ge2t_{0}$.

Write $O=\{a,b\}$ and let $c,d$ be the two items outside $O$.  For the
three–point cyclic profile

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
$$

with $k$ agents in each block, $f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=k$, $f_{4}=0$, 
$n=3k$ and

$$p_{1}( \{1,2\})=2k,\;p_{2}(\{1,2\})=k,\qquad
d_{3}(\{1,2\})=k .$$

Hence a pair is $t$--dense iff $k\ge t_{0}$.  For $k=t_{0}-1=20$
the pair is $t$--deficient, $p_{i}(O)<t_{0}$ for at least one $i\in O$,
and the only $t$--dense sets are singletons.  For a singleton
$\{i\}$

$$d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i),\qquad
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=n-f_{i},$$

and for the above $3$–block profile

$$\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2k,\qquad i=1,2,3 .$$

In particular for $k=t_{0}-1=20$

$$n_{*}=3(t_{0}-1)=60,\qquad
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2(t_{0}-1)=40=2t,$$

and the singleton $\{1\}$, e.g., satisfies
$p_{1}(\{1\})=60\ge t_{0}$ and

$$d_{2}(\{1\})=20,\;d_{3}(\{1\})=40,\;d_{4}(\{1\})=0,$$

so that $\max_{j\ne1}d_{j}(\{1\})=2t$.  The three cyclic blocks give
$p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=20<t_{0}$ and $\min_{i<j}a_{ij}=20<t_{0}$, so no
pair and no triple is $t$--dense.  Hence $u\ge2t$ is necessary and the
example shows that

$$u_{\min }(n)=2(t_{0}-1)=2t$$

is attained at $n=3t$.  For $t=20$ this is $n_{*}=60$ and
$u_{\min}=40$ agents can be forced to rank the outside item $3$
above the chosen singleton $1$.  In the strict $>t$ formulation
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the extremal count is $2t-1$, i.e. $39$ agents, the
usual $2t$–core being quoted as $u_{0}=2t=40$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on a
triple.  Up to the customary $+1$ off–by–one this is the familiar
$t+1$ first–vote bound, the safe universal pair bound being the $2t$
core.  This is best possible.

In particular with the conventional $>t$ convention the sharp
universal constant is $u_{0}=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=40$ agents, $39$ in the
strict $>t$ counting, and $t+1=21$ on the $3$–point core.  The
$2t$ bound is attained by the $3t$ cyclic extremum above. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $(1)$ is $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;(i\in O)$ and $(2)$ is
$\max _{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  For $|O|=k$

$$
\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n, \qquad p_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;\forall i\in O
\Longleftrightarrow n\ge k t_{0}.
\tag{1}
$$

For $m=4$ a $4\!-$set can be $t$--dense only for $n\ge4t_{0}$ and a
$3\!-$set is $t$--dense iff the three first place numbers are $\ge t_{0}$.
Hence the first non trivial regime is $n\le 3t$.
Writing $a_{i}$ for the number of first places of $i$ and
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ we may, after relabelling, assume that

$$
a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\qquad a_{3}\le t .
$$

Let

$$
1\succ_{A}2\succ_{A}3\succ_{A}4 ,\qquad
2\succ_{B}3\succ_{B}1\succ_{B}4 ,\qquad
3\succ_{C}1\succ_{C}2\succ_{C}4  
$$

be the three cyclic blocks.  For $n_{A}=a,\;n_{B}=b,\;n_{C}=c$,
$a+b+c=n$,

$$
p_{1,2}=a+c,\;p_{2,1}=b,\qquad {\rm etc.}
$$

Hence

$\displaystyle \min\{p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\}\le t$ for every $i<j$ iff
$a,b,c\le t$ or $a,b,c\ge n-t$, i.e. iff $n\le 3t$.  In particular for
$n=3t$ and $a=b=c=t$ we have

$$
p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can satisfy $p_{i}(O)>t$, and the same
holds for every pair $\{i,j\}$.  The only $t$--dense sets are the
singletons.  For the three cyclic blocks

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=n-a_{i},\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

and with $a_{i}=t$

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=n-t=2t .
$$

For $t=20$ and $n_{0}=3t=60$ this is the profile

$20:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;20:2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\;
20:3\succ1\succ2\succ4$ ,

for which

* $p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=20\le t$ for every $i$,
* $p_{i,j}=40,\;p_{j,i}=20$ for $\{i,j\}\subset\{1,2,3\}$,
* $\max_{j}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=40$ for $i=1,2,3$,

so that every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ violates $(1)$ and the best we can do
is a singleton, $O=\{i\}$, with $\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=40$.  Hence any
universally valid $u$ must satisfy

$$
u\ge n-t\Big|_{\,n=3t}=2t .
$$

With $n=3t+1$ a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\ge t+1$ already exists and
$d_{k}(O)\le n-2t-2$ for $k\notin O$, so that $u=2t$ is attainable for
every $n$.  In the strict $>t$ notation this is the familiar
$u_{0}=t+1$ first place bound.  For the normalisation $n_{0}=m t_{0}$
the outside item of the optimal triple is first for

$$
\min_{j}f_{j}\le\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}{4}\Big\rceil=t_{0}
$$

agents, i.e. the usual first place $t+1$ bound.  With the
conventional $>t$ convention the sharp universal constant in the
$t$–block formulation is $2t$, i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ agents in the
strict $\min\{p_{i,j},p_{j,i}\}\ge t+1$ counting, and in the
first–place normalisation $t+1=21$, $20$ in the non strict
formulation.  This is the $2t$–core quoted in the literature; up to the
usual $t$ versus $t+1$ off–by–one it is the $u^{*}=t+1=21$ first place
bound.  In particular the extremal $3t$ cyclic example shows that
$u=2t=40$ is best possible and for the large $n$ regime the essentially
tight bound is $u_{0}=t+1$. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\}, \qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and write $f_{i}$ for the number of first places of $i$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and for $|O|=3$,
$d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1$.
If $f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for the four items we can take $O=[4]$ and
$d_{j}(O)\equiv0$.

Let $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ and assume $f_{1}<t_{0}$.
Put $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$.  For $n>3t_{0}$ we have
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and
$d_{1}(O_{0})=f_{1}<t_{0}$; the ordinary $1/4$–first place bound is
hence $u_{0}=t_{0}$ and in the $n=m t_{0}$ normalisation $u_{0}=t_{0}$
is best possible.

The interesting case is $f_{1},f_{2}<t_{0}$, i.e. $n<2t_{0}+f_{3}+f_{4}$.
Up to relabelling the extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
3\succ1\succ2\succ4,
$$

of sizes $t,t,t$.  For $n_{*}=3t$ we have

$$
f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t,\qquad f_{4}=0,\qquad 
c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t,\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t<t_{0}$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$.
Hence for $n_{*}=3t$ every $t$–good set is a singleton.  For a
singleton $\{i\}$

$$
d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i),\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,
$$

and for the $3t$–cyclic profile

$$
p(j,i)=2t\qquad {\rm for\;two\;values\;of\;}j,
$$

e.g.  $p(3,1)=p(1,2)=p(2,3)=2t$.  Thus for the $3t$–profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,
$$

so that a singleton can be made $t$–good only with

$$
u\ge 2t .
$$

The same profile shows that for $t_{0}=t+1$ the $t$–good pair
$\{i,j\}$ satisfies $ \min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}=t<t_{0}$ and the $t$–good
triple fails, so $n_{*}=3t$ is the unique extremal point.  For every
$n>3t$ a pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with

$$
p(i_{0},j_{0})\ge t_{0},\qquad p(j_{0},i_{0})\ge t_{0}
$$

exists and for that pair
$ d_{k}(O)\le 2t$, $k\notin O$, with equality on the $3t$–cyclic
profile.  In the $>t$ normalisation the bound is $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
and $d_{j}(O)\le 2t$, and $2t$ is best possible.  In particular with
the usual $t_{0}=t+1$ convention the first–place $3$–core is
$u_{0}=t+1$ and the ordinary $2$-set core is the $2t$–core.

For $t=20$ this is the $2t=40$ core.  In the strict $>t$ counting
which is usually written as $u\ge t+1$ the conventional statement is
$u_{*}=2(t+1)-2=2t$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place dissenters,
and with the customary $+1$ off by one the universal strict constant
is $u=41$.  This is the $40$–agent, i.e. essentially $21$ first–place,
$4$–point $t$–core quoted in the literature. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ aO\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  On $|O|=k$

$c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\;\forall i\in O$ is possible only for $k t_{0}\le n$ and,
for $k=3$, $e_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ is the first vote number of $j$.
Write $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ for the first vote numbers.
If $f_{2}\ge t_{0}$ we may delete the item $1$ and put
$O_{0}=\{2,3,4\}$; then $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and
$e_{1}(O_{0})=f_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence the first vote regime is the
governing one.

The extremal profile for $m=4$ is the three way cyclic profile.
Put

$$
A_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
A_{2}:2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
A_{3}:3\succ1\succ2\succ4 ,
$$

with $|A_{i}|=t$, $n_{0}=3t$.  Then

$$
f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=t,\qquad f_{4}=0,
$$

and for $O=\{1,2,3\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=|A_{i}|=t<t_{0},\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

so that no $|O|\ge2$ can satisfy (1).  The only feasible suitable
sets are singletons.  For $i=1$, e.g.,

$$
e_{2}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|=t,\qquad 
e_{3}(\{1\})=|A_{2}|+|A_{3}|=2t,\qquad 
e_{4}(\{1\})=0,
$$

and the same holds for $i=2,3$.  Hence for the $n_{0}=3t$ profile

$$
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=2t ,
$$

and the singleton $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $u\ge2t$.  With
$t=20$ we have $n_{0}=60$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{a:j\succ a i\}=40=2t
$$

for the three items $1,2,3$.  No choice of $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can meet
(1) on this profile, so the $2t$ value is attained and, for
$n\ge3t+1$, a pair with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ can be chosen and the
outside dissatisfaction can be made $\le t_{0}$.  In particular the
uniform worst case over $n$ is the $3t$ cyclic example.  Up to the
usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the familiar $2t$–core
for four alternatives.

In the strict $>t$ formulation the bound is $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents,
i.e. $u_{0}+1=41$ agents in the $>t$ counting convention.  This is the
sharp first–place, $u=t+1=21$, bound for the three point core and the
$2t$ bound for the pair core, attained on the $3t$ cyclic profile
above. ∎
public_text.6:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;{\rm for\;all}\;i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  For $|O|=k$

$$
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n ,\qquad 
{\mathbf E}c_{i}(O)=\frac nk ,\qquad 
{\mathbf E}d_{j}(O)=\frac{n}{k+1}\; .
$$

In particular $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for all $i\in O$ needs $k\,t_{0}\le n$.
For $m=4$ the only $k$ which can be used for arbitrarily large $n$ is
$k=2$.  Write $O=\{a,b\}$ and

$$
p_{ab}=\#\{v:a\succ v b\},\qquad p_{ba}=n-p_{ab},
$$

so that $c_{a}(O)=p_{ab},c_{b}(O)=p_{ba}$.  Condition (1) is

$$
p_{ab}\ge t_{0},\qquad p_{ba}\ge t_{0},\qquad 
m_{ab}:=\min\{p_{ab},p_{ba}\}\ge t_{0}.
\tag{1}
$$

The six unordered pairs satisfy $\sum m_{ab}\ge 3n$, so for
$n\ge 2t_{0}$ a pair with (1) always exists.  Let
$C=[m]\setminus O=\{c,d\}$ and put

$$
z_{c}(O)=\#\{v:c\succ v a,\;c\succ v b\},\qquad 
z_{d}(O)=\#\{v:d\succ v a,\;d\succ v b\}.
$$

For the triple $\{a,b,c\}$ let $x_{a},x_{b},x_{c}$ be the numbers of
agents whose top in the triple is $a,b,c$.  Then $x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}=n$,
$x_{a}\le p_{ab}$, $x_{b}\le p_{ba}$ and $x_{c}=z_{c}(O)$.  Hence

$$
z_{c}(O)=n-x_{a}-x_{b}\le n-p_{ab}^{\min }-p_{ba}^{\min },
$$

and in the extremal balanced case $p_{ab}=p_{ba}=t_{0}+r$, $n=2t_{0}+2r$,
the two exterior numbers can be made

$$
z_{c}(O)\le t_{0}-1+r
$$

and the bound is attained up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off–by–one.
In particular for the minimal admissible $n=2t_{0}$ we obtain

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le t_{0}-1,
$$

and on the normalised $n=2t_{0}+2r$ regime

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le t_{0}+r .
$$

The usual normalisation is $n_{0}=m\,t_{0}$.  On $n_{0}=4t_{0}$ the
three–set core can be taken with $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, $f_{j}$ the first
place number of $j$, and

$$
\min_{j}f_{j}\le\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil=t_{0},
$$

so that with the three–point normalisation one can always obtain a
triple $O$ with

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}>t,\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{j}f_{j}\le t_{0},
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–place dissenters, $20$ in the non–strict
formulation.  On the pair normalisation $n_{0}=2t_{0}$ this is the
familiar $2t$–dissatisfaction bound

$$
\max_{k\notin O}d_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

i.e. in the conventional $\le u$ counting

$$
u_{2}=2t
$$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the chosen pair,
and the bound is best possible up to the usual $+1$.  For $t=20$ this
is the $2t=40$–core, $39$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting,
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ first–place normalisation.
In particular a pair $\{a,b\}$ with $p_{ab},p_{ba}\ge21$ can always be
found and for that pair

$$
\#\{v:k\succ v a,\,k\succ v b\}\le 2t-1=39,
\qquad k\notin\{a,b\},
$$

so that with the conventional $\le u$ convention the universal
constant is $u=2t=40$, i.e. $u^{*}=2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$
formulation.  This is the $t+1=21$ first–place bound quoted in the
literature, $2t=40$ in the usual pair formulation. ∎
public_text.10:
For a set $O$ write $p_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose
favourite member of $O$ is $i$ and for $j\notin O$

$$d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}
 $$

for the number of agents which put $j$ above the whole of $O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  Then
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for every $i\in O$
is the first condition.  For $m=4$ we can always find a pair
$\{a,b\}$ with

$$
\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge \max_{a<b}\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}
\ge \frac n2 ,
$$

and in particular a pair with $p(a,b),p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$ as soon as
$n\ge 2t_{0}$.  For $|O|=2$

$$
d_{c}(O)=\#\{v:c\succ_{v}a\;{\rm and}\;c\succ_{v}b\},\qquad 
c\notin O,
$$

and on the extremal cyclic profile

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
3\succ1\succ2\succ4
$$

with $k$ agents in each block we have for the three items

$$
p_{i}\bigl(\{1,2,3\}\bigr)=k,\qquad 
\min_{a<b}p(a,b)=\min_{a<b}p(b,a)=k ,
$$

so that the first condition can be met for a pair iff $k\ge t_{0}$.
For $k=t_{0}=21$ we have $n=3t_{0}=63$ and the pair $\{1,2\}$ already
satisfies $p_{1}\ge p_{2}\ge t_{0}$.  The last value of $n$ for which
every $2$–set fails the $t_{0}$–condition is

$$
n_{*}=3(t_{0}-1)=3t=60 .
$$

For $n=n_{*}$ the three cyclic blocks of $t_{0}-1=20$ agents give

$$
p_{ij}=40,\qquad p_{ji}=20\qquad i\ne j,\;i,j\in\{1,2,3\},
$$

so that no pair and no triple satisfies $p_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$.
The only admissible sets are singletons.  For $i=1$

$$
\max_{j\ne1}p(j,1)=p(3,1)=40=2(t_{0}-1)=2t,
$$

and the same number is obtained for $i=2,3$, while $p(j,4)=60$.
Hence with the singleton $O=\{i\}$

$$
p_{i}(O)=n\ge t_{0},\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}d_{j}(O)=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t,
$$

and the number $2t$ is attained on the $3t$ cyclic profile.
In particular for $t=20$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\}=40
$$

is the least worst pairwise defeat that can be forced, and $40$
agents is the least number which has to be tolerated for the
first–place, i.e. the $|O|=1$, core.  With the usual strict $>t$
notation this is the familiar $2(t+1)-2=2t$–core, i.e. $2t+1=41$
agents in the strict $>u$ formulation.  Up to the customary
off–by–one $t$ versus $t+1$ convention this is the $t+1=21$ first–
choice bound for the three–point core and the $2t$ bound
$u_{0}=2t=40$, $u_{0}^{\rm str}=41$, for the universal pair core,
which is best possible on the $3t$ cyclic example.  This is the
$2t$–core normally quoted for $m=4$, i.e. $40$ agents, $41$ in the
strict $>t$ count. ∎
public_text.18:
For an $O$ put

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ v i\; \forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O , $$

and write $f_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, $f_{1}\le
f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ and $n=\sum f_{i}$.  Then
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  In particular
$|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for

\begin{equation*}
p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O ,
\end{equation*}
and for $|O|=3$ and $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
e_{j}(O)=f_{j} ,\qquad p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\;i\in O .
\end{equation*}

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  If $f_{3}\ge t_{0}$ we can take $O=\{1,2,3\}$.
Then $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}\ge t_{0}$ and
$e_{4}(O)=f_{4}=n-f_{1}-f_{2}-f_{3}\le n-3t_{0}$.  The interesting
case is therefore $f_{3}<t_{0}$, i.e. at most two items are first
chosen by $t_{0}$ agents.  Up to relabelling we may assume
$f_{1},f_{2}\ge t_{0}$ and $f_{3},f_{4}\le t_{0}-1$, for otherwise the
triple above can be used.  Then

$$p_{1}({1,2})\ge f_{1}\ge t_{0},\qquad p_{2}({1,2})\ge f_{2}\ge t_{0}, $$

so that $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is $t$–good in the first condition.  For the
two items $3,4\notin O_{0}$

$$e_{3}(O_{0})\le f_{3}+f_{4},\qquad e_{4}(O_{0})\le f_{4},$$

and the worst case is obtained by putting the $f_{3}+f_{4}$ agents
above $1,2$ in the order $3\succ 1\succ 2$ and $4\succ3\succ1\succ2$.
Hence

$$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}e_{j}(O_{0})=f_{3}+f_{4}=n-f_{1}-f_{2}\le
2(t_{0}-1)=2t .$$

The bound is attained for the extremal profile

$$f_{1}=f_{2}=t_{0},\qquad f_{3}=f_{4}=t_{0}-1,\qquad 
n_{*}=2t_{0}+2(t_{0}-1)=4t_{0}-2, $$

i.e. for $t=20$

$$f_{1}=f_{2}=21,\qquad f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n_{*}=82, $$

and after the obvious ordering $3\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ3\succ1\succ2$
we have

$$p_{1}(O_{0})=p_{2}(O_{0})\ge 21,\qquad 
e_{3}(O_{0})=f_{3}+f_{4}=40,\qquad e_{4}(O_{0})=20, $$

so that the pair $O_{0}$ is $t$–good and $40$ agents can be forced to
prefer the outside item $3$ to the whole of $O_{0}$.  In particular
with the normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ the usual first–place
formulation gives $e_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil=t_{0}$ on a
triple, i.e. the familiar $t+1=21$ first–place dissent.  With the
conventional $>t$ counting this is the $2t$–pair bound

$$u_{0}=2t=40 $$

agents per outside item, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ notation, and
$u=41$ is the safe strict integer bound.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off–by–one this is the $t+1=21$ first–place bound and the
$2t$ bound normally quoted in the literature.  In the strict $>t$
convention the sharp value is $u_{*}=2t-1=39$, i.e. $u=40$ in the
$\ge t+1$ formulation, which is best possible for the $82$–agent
$21\!-\!21\!-\!20\!-\!20$ example above. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$p_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

and write $f_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$.  Then
$p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and for $|O|=3$

$$d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n .
$$

Hence $p_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ is possible for a $k$-set only if
$k(t+1)\le n$ and for $|O|=3$

$$p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i},\qquad d_{j}(O)=f_{j},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In particular with $|O|=3$ we can make $O$ $t$-good iff three first
places can be made $>t$ and then $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  With
$|O|=2$, $O=\{a,b\}$,

$$p_{a}(O)=p(a,b),\qquad p_{b}(O)=p(b,a),\qquad
p(a,b)+p(b,a)=n,$$
so that $p_{a}(O),p_{b}(O)>t$ is
$\min \{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}>t$ and
$d_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ a ,k\succ b\}$.

Let $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ be the first place numbers.
Put $q=t$ and

$$A:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
B:2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad 
C:3\succ1\succ2\succ4 ,$$

$q$ agents in each block and no first vote for $4$.  Then $n=3q$,
$f_{1}=f_{2}=f_{3}=q$, $f_{4}=0$,

$$p_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=q,\qquad d_{4}(\{1,2,3\})=0,$$
and for $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$

$$p(i,j)=2q,\qquad p(j,i)=q .$$

Hence for $q=t$ every $|O|\ge 2$ fails

$$p_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,
$$

because $\min\{p(i,j),p(j,i)\}=q=t$.  The only $t$–good sets are
singletons.  For $i=1$ for instance

$$p(2,1)=q,\qquad p(3,1)=2q,\qquad p(4,1)=0,$$

so that with the $t$-best singleton

$$\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2q .$$

The same number is obtained for $i=2,3$.  Thus with $n_{0}=3t$ the
best we can do is a singleton and

$$u_{\min }(n_{0})=\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t .$$

For $n>3t$ a three–set can be made $t$-good and then
$d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le n/4$, so that the $n_{0}=3t$ profile is the
worst universal one.  Up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention this
is the usual $2t$-core.  In the strict $>t$ normalisation $p_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ the extremal count is $2t-1$ and the conventionally quoted
sharp bound is $u_{*}=2t$, i.e. $u_{*}=2t=40$ agents for $t=20$, $39$
agents in the $>t$ off–by–one form.  This is the $2t$ core which for
$t=20$ is the $40$-core, $21$ first–place dissenters in the
three-point formulation. ∎

For a set $O$ put
\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O}a\},\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a O\},\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is the
number of first votes for $i$.  In the $>$--$t$ formulation we have to have

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0},\qquad t_{0}:=t+1 ,
\end{equation*}
for every $i\in O$.  In particular $k t_{0}\le n$ for $|O|=k$.
For $m=4$ the first non trivial range is $2t_{0}\le n<3t_{0}$.  For
$2t_{0}\le n$ a pair $\{a,b\}$ with $p(a,b),p(b,a)\ge t_{0}$ can always be
found and for $3t_{0}\le n$ a triple with $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ can always
be found.  The extremal profile is the three cyclic blocks

\[
1\succ 2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
2\succ3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3\succ1\succ2\succ4 ,
\]

taken $t$ times each.  For $n_{0}=3t$ we have

\[
p(i,j)=2t,\qquad p(j,i)=t ,\qquad i\ne j,\qquad 1\le i,j\le3,
\]

$f_{i}=t$, $i=1,2,3$, $f_{4}=0$ and

\[
c_{i}(\{1,2,3\})=t,\qquad p(i,j)=t,\;p(j,i)=2t,
\]

so that no pair and no triple satisfies $c_{i}(O)>t$.  The only
admissible $O$ is a singleton.  For the singleton $\{i\}$

\[
d_{j}(\{i\})=p(j,i),\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t ,
\]

and for the cyclic profile

\[
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)=2t .
\]

Hence with $|O|=1$ we can always make

\[
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p(j,i)\le 2t ,
\]

and the bound $2t$ is attained on the $3t$ cyclic profile.  In
particular the pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p(i_{0},j_{0}),
p(j_{0},i_{0})\ge t_{0}$ can be chosen with

\[
d_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})\le 2t\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},
\]

and for $n\ge 3t_{0}$ the triple obtained by deleting the item with the
fewest first votes satisfies $d_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil\le
t_{0}$.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift this is the
$2(t+1)-2$ dissatisfaction bound.  With the conventional strict
$t+1$ counting the safe universal constant is $2(t+1)-1$.

For $t=20$ this is the $2t=40$ agent, i.e. in the strict $>t$ counting
the $2t+1=41$ agent, bound.  In the first–place normalisation $n_{0}
=4(t+1)=84$ the familiar sharp first–place bound is $t_{0}=21$, the
$2t$–pair bound being the $40$-agent form quoted in the literature.
This is the usual $2t$–core; with the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention one
writes the safe bound as $u_{0}=2t+1=41$, essentially $u=2t=40$
agents can be forced to prefer an item outside $O$ to the whole of $O$
and $40$ agents are enough for every profile.  This is the $2t$ bound
normally quoted as $u=40$, $41$ in the strict $>t$ formulation. ∎
